speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE STUDY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the fall of the Canadian dollar has had more impact on the Canadian economy than any budget that has been introduced in the life of this government, but the plight of the dollar has been kept away from debate in parliament, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That the government make an immediate reference to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs to allow for a full discussion of the reasons for and the impact of the falling dollar, and that the committee be empowered to call witnesses, including the minister, the governor of the Bank of Canada, representatives of the chartered banks and representatives of the financial institutions which have acted for the government in their foreign exchange transactions.

subsubtopic: STEPS TO ENSURE FOREIGN-OWNED COMPANIES BECOME GOOD CORPORATE CITIZENS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to move a motion under Standing Order 43.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), in Toronto during the weekend, with regard to guidelines to control the operation of foreign-owned companies in Canada, is quoted by the Canadian Press as saying:
Very little effort has been made to inform foreign-owned corporations of the rules, and certainly nobody has ever tried to check whether there's been any compliance. The frustrating thing about all of this is that I had a tough Fight in cabinet to get my guidelines approved, and it's all come to nothing.
Also, a senior official in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is quoted by the Canadian Press as saying:
Everyone you ask here about the Gillespie guidelines gives a Trudeau-like shrug and a broad grin, and it seems nobody's given it a second thought since 1975.

That this House direct the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to ensure that foreign-owned companies are advised without delay what their responsibilities are as good Canadian corporate citizens, and that steps are taken by his department to ensure these responsibilities are carried out in a satisfactory manner, so that Canadians may derive the greatest possible benefit from the foreign capital invested in this country.

speechtext:

In view of the fact that the CBC must faithfully report all newsworthy items, always adopt an unbiased attitude when broadcasting conflicting approaches to important events, and make a point of maintaining a non-partisan balance between the various opinions expressed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the Speaker of the House send a letter to the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to congratulate him for the coverage which was given to the Pepin-Robarts report on the eleven o'clock news last Thursday night and Friday night, and again during a special program where the activities of the week were summarized; to congratulate him, I said, for having wilfully failed to broadcast the views of the Social Credit Party of Canada.

ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW NATIONAL ENERGY POLICY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Because of the tremendous increase in the cost of energy in Nova Scotia and other eastern provinces resulting from the escalation in the world price of the oil required for generation of electric power, some industrial plants are unable to continue in operation in competition with those in provinces with lower energy costs. That this House direct the government to consider the establishment of a new national energy policy which would provide assistance so that the cost of energy to industrial and other users in one province will not exceed the national average cost of energy.

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister, who must know that when the questions that he was referring to were attempted to be asked, they were ruled out of order at the committee.
The Prime Minister seems to want to fill us in on what is happening in the world. Can he indicate why the Canadian dollar, in relation to the American dollar, has fallen 15 per cent in the past two years, while the Japanese yen has gone up 77 per cent in relation to the Canadian dollar, the British pound is up 36 per cent and the deutschemark up 51 per cent? Why has the international market passed such a devastating verdict on Canada to make ours the softest currency of any of the industrialized countries?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this may call for a long answer, but I will begin to give it. If you allow me, Mr. Speaker, I will try and explain some of the basics of economics to the hon. member.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext: When a country chooses to protect its currency by having very restrictive monetary policies which slow down the growth of the economy, it can indeed have a high-value currency. The problem is that this tends to create unemployment.

speechtext: Like Japan and Germany.

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext: The hon. member says, "Like Japan and Germany".

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext:
The point is there is no unemployment in those countries.

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext:
The hon. member says there is no unemployment there. When you can ship your unemployment out of the country, as is the case, for example, in Switzerland or Germany-it was the case when they were protecting their currencies-it is reasonably easy to have a restrictive growth and ship your unemployment abroad. Then you have a strong currency.
In the case of Japan, they do not ship their people abroad; they force the employers to keep them employed, and the workers in the plant take reduced salaries in order that everyone keeps working. There are various techniques that have been used, about which members opposite do not seem to be informed. However, you have to make a choice. If you want to continue creating jobs, as this country has, and it has created 428,000 jobs year over year-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext: -this means not following the restrictive monetary policies that some of these countries have followed. It has been our choice to make sure that Canada continues to produce jobs at a rate which is faster than any of the industrialized societies.

speechtext: I have just answered that. Of course, when the dollar falls, the price of imported products-

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES
speechtext: Canadian products.

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR IN RELATION TO OTHER CURRENCIES

-the price of imported goods and substitutes for them tends to differ; they cost more to the consumer. In terms of exports, it means that Canadian goods are more competitive on international markets; that we are selling more on international markets and consequently creating more jobs in Canada. This is one of the beneficial effects of the lower dollar.
Of course, unless we are going into a two-price export products structure, which I do not believe the opposition is advocating, it does mean Canadians will be paying more for goods which are higher priced on international markets.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the Prime Minister. I note with interest his new-found concern with job creation. In that context, I should like to say, as a preamble to my questions, that in 1975 the then minister of industry, trade and commerce tabled a set of guidelines designed to ensure that benefits to Canada from the performance of foreign-controlled firms would be improved. Among these were increased research and development at home, increased exports and further processing of natural resources: in short, more jobs.
Considering that senior officials in that department confirmed yesterday that absolutely no monitoring of foreign-controlled firms had been done since 1975 to ensure that these objectives were fulfilled, why has the government so completely failed in the stated course of action it established almost four years ago?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext: The question is somewhat contradictory. The Leader of the New Democratic Party speaks about my "new-found concern" for creating jobs. I can tell him that throughout the seventies this government and the Canadian economy have had the best record of any industrialized nation in terms of creating jobs.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext:
That is a matter of statistical record. I see the Leader of the New Democratic Party shrugs about that. He does not like performance; he just like words about the future. Regarding the future, these guidelines were established by the then minister of industry, trade and commerce precisely in order to contribute to a larger pool of job creation. The figures show he has been partly successful.
The hon. member says there has been no monitoring. Of course there has been monitoring; there has been monitoring of all the firms reviewed by the Foreign Investment Review Agency. The very statement from which he has read indicates that FIRA has beefed-up its capacity for monitoring the application of such guidelines. As far as other areas are concerned, I take the point that there has not been sufficient monitoring. If some firms say they have not been following the guidelines, and others say they have we shall take note of it and make sure that more and more of them do follow the guidelines promulgated at the time by the then minister of industry.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext: The Prime Minister says the government has created more jobs than other countries. The reality is that it had to do so because of the higher level of unemployment than other countries-a million short in terms of jobs.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext:
Very convoluted.

January 30, 1979

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has indicated that FIRA rates the performance of newly-established foreign investment. That, as we all know, is inadequate.
The question had nothing to do with that. The question pertains to the existing foreign-owned firms to which the then minister applied his guidelines in 1975 but which are not being enforced now.
Will the Prime Minister confirm that there has been no enforcement or monitoring, and will he therefore admit that his own government's inaction has produced many fewer jobs than it could have?

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find that the Leader of the New Democratic Party is not very convincing when he says "Sure we have created more jobs than any other society, but we have done so because we have had to". Of course we want to create as many jobs as possible but that is what we have done. To say that we had to do it is not any form of praise or blame, because there are many other countries with very high rates of unemployment which should be creating jobs but which are not.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext: Like Germany or Japan? Which ones have high unemployment?

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA
speechtext:
I just spoke about two particular countries which reduced their unemployment figures by sending their unemployed back to Portugal, Spain or Yugoslavia. We do not do that in Canada. Workers come here and they get jobs, but we do not exile them just because they become unemployed. This is not our way of doing things, and I do not suppose it is something the Leader of the New Democratic Party would propose.
We have these guidelines. They apply in the case of newly-established firms which came under FIRA. They apply to the others. If they have not been applied with enough force and stength, I will ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to report on this and to make sure that the guidelines are adhered to. I merely say that the promulgation of those guidelines must have produced some results, since it coincided with the period when Canada created jobs at a faster rate than that of any other industrialized society.

subtopic: MONITORING OF PERFORMANCE OF FOREIGN-CONTROLLED COMPANIES IN CANADA

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, but in his absence I would address it to the right hon. Prime Minister.
Statistics Canada yesterday released figures showing an average weekly wage increase of a little over 6 per cent, compared to a 9 per cent increase in the consumer price index last year. Since this represents an annual wage loss of $365 for the average worker in Canada, I want to follow up on a question posed yesterday by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, and ask the Prime Minister if he is aware that corporations which were represented at his Friday meeting have experienced astronomical and scandalous profit increases over the last year. For example, Noranda Mines had a 117 per cent increase. I have these figures, which I will make available to the Prime Minister.
If the Prime Minister is aware of these profit increases, will he inform the House why he did not ask the corporations concerned to reduce their prices so that Canadians do not have to face high cost of living increases over the next few years?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

This is a suggestion which will be carried forth by this government.
In so far as the earlier statistics given by the hon. member are concerned, of course they are right if he just takes last year. If he takes the period of three years during which controls endured, he will see that the workers' wages over that period were above the increase in the cost of living. Indeed, if he looks at the past ten years, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance reminded us yesterday, he will see that real disposable incomes in Canada went up 52 per cent which, incidentally, is about twice as high as they went up in the United States over the same period.

The House resumed from Monday, January 29, 1979, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde (for Mr. Reid) that Bill C-9, respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night, I started my speech very late and pointed out that I could make only preliminary remarks. But even those preliminary remarks I did not have time to complete. I was more specifically commenting on the speech made earlier by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). He said yesterday that there was no national unity problem and that our difficulties were rather of an economic nature.
Yesterday, I said what I thought of the perception the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi has of matters of national unity, but I should also like to mention that he insists that the most important issue today is one of economics. I do not disagree with that, Mr. Speaker. Economic matters must command the attention of the government. However, I want to remind the hon. member that we deal with those matters in due course and that this government can easily act simultaneously on several fronts.
That national unity is a major problem at this time cannot be denied. We have in Quebec, as I pointed out yesterday, a government intent upon dividing Canada, that is, upon separating one of the Canadian provinces from confederation. If that does not constitute an important problem for Canada, I wonder what does. Personally, I feel that even though it is true that national unity must not be the only matter with which we must deal, it certainly is of considerable if not capital significance in economic matters. Consequently, that national issue must be discussed and we must do everything possible to solve the problems facing us at this time.
I believe the government has made an effort in that direction by introducing in the House this legislation on referen-
January 30, 1979

dums. At this point of the debate, I feel it is important to clear up the situation. We see the opposition rising against this legislation on the referendum on the pretext that it could be abused. I note the opposition refuses to acknowledge that we have set out in the bill some limitations to the use of the referendum once enacted. One of those limitations lies in the fact that its life is limited to five years, a period during which we hope to have been successful in settling our national unity problem and perhaps even carried out a constitutional reform we could put before the people and on which we could hold a referendum. On the other hand, the opposition refuses to acknowledge that we have limited the referendum to constitutional matters only. They refuse to acknowledge that, yet fail to spell out what they think is something other than constitutional matters. And they state we could abuse that political instrument to the point where we would be legislating by referendum.
In this regard, I have a comment I would like to make about the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. He is opposed, and rightly so, to our legislating by referendum, yet he recommended last night that we legislate by public poll. Here is what he said in substance: There is no need for any referendum. Governments enjoy the power to conduct public polls even more important than those conducted by the Gallup Institute, in order to know exactly where people stand on a question like national unity.
I must say I found some boldness in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi when he called upon this House, with tears in his eyes, to show better respect for democracy. Which is more democratic, Mr. Speaker, legislating by polls or, from time to time and in extremely limited circumstances, putting to the people a referendum on a central issue of concern to them? What the opposition would like in fact and what they imply when suggesting they are against the referendum is that they are against the idea of asking the people's views on constitutional reform. I for one feel that if we were to obtain the provinces' agreement on the current constitutional negotiations, the outline of the resulting constitutional remodelling should be submitted to the people through a referendum, and this is why we are putting the legislation forward.
What must be realized is that the bill had its inception in circumstances that were quite special, namely the election that occurred in the province of Quebec on November 15, 1976. Those political circumstances called for unusual political responses. The referendum bill is one of those unusual responses that also meets a specific need I shall be explaining in a moment, and that is also designed to address the larger question of constitutional reform.
Listening to the opposition I see they lack the flexibility, the kind of imagination that would allow them to easily turn around in tighter political situations. They lack the understanding, the basic sense of strategy that would allow them to
Referenda
join us in accepting this proposal to give the authority to hold referenda, either in the country as a whole or in the province of Quebec only, for a limited period and on constitutional matters only. Under the circumstances the reason becomes apparent why in the race for power they can never make it at the finish line: they are incapable of what I would call elementary analysis of a political situation. If they were now to make a cold-headed review of the facts, they would look at this proposal with a minimum of objectivity. But the truth is Progressive Conservatives have had no understanding whatsoever of what goes on in the province of Quebec, as we have long since realized, but they do not quite grasp what is going on in the rest of the country either. We had examples in the suggestions made recently by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), who was only echoing statements made much earlier by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
I suspect that this type of statement was suggested to the hon. member for Rosedale by Mr. Payette, the candidate whom the Progressive Conservatives have just recruited and, I warn the opposition, whose political options are not very clear. Following the statements of Mr. Ryan who quite properly took offence at what the hon. member for Rosedale said, I would say to the hon. member, an ex-mayor, that he should have taken the time, when he was mayor of Toronto, to make a few visits in the province of Quebec, especially in the city of Montreal; then he could have understood what is happening there, he could have improved his political education so that he would have been a bit more mature when he came to the House and he might have known better than to make such statements.
This was a rare occasion for him to fraternize with the people of Montreal, with Quebeckers, and to get informed on what is really happening in the province of Quebec, but he did not do so and now he sits here in the federal parliament without knowing the real problems of Canada and without having grasped the national dimension of these problems. What is the actual situation in Quebec which justifies this legislation on the referendum? I am going to sum it up briefly because I do not want to dwell too much on it and above all because many of these things have already been said. When it was elected, the Parti Quebecois promised the Quebec people it would hold a referendum on the independence issue. Soon after, realizing that this measure was not quite popular, it began to say that it would hold the referendum within a year. It then stated that it could no longer put a definite date on it. Finally it declared that it might even wait until after the coming federal election.
One can easily say that the Parti Quebecois is just procrastinating and those who analyse the situation will see quite clearly that if the Parti Quebecois hesitates so much it is because it knows quite well that it will not win the referendum. So what is it doing in the meanwhile? Well, for the Parti Quebecois it is crucial to gain time, because it has devised a strategy whereby in gaining time it could project a moderate image of itself before the people and make them believe that it
2704

January 30, 1979
Referenda
is now quite in favour of outright independence, and it could make all kinds of gestures which would tend to mystify the population. Furthermore, it is quite consciously creating some ambiguity around one of several questions which could perhaps turn out to be contridactory and which could be asked when the referendum takes place. The last invention devised by the Parti Quebecois in order to confuse the people has been to declare itself as following the path and the tradition of all the heads of parties in the province of Quebec and of all the former premiers of Quebec up to this day. It claims merely to be acting in conformity with the traditional attitude of the province of Quebec.
Yet, though it claims to be consistent with the previous stands of the province of Quebec, to the best of my knowledge the preceding governements have never advocated the separation of Quebec from the rest of the country. Yet such is the goal of the Parti Quebecois. This is what it has been saying within the province of Quebec but at the same time Mr. Rene Levesque goes to Washington to explain that his goal is independence for Quebec and to try to convince the public there that such a move constitutes no threat for the United States or the rest of Canada. He therefore adopts a federalist approach when he addresses his fellow Quebeckers or at certain federal-provincial conferences and on the other hand he takes a separatist approach when speaking abroad. It is exactly the opposite that is true. The Quebec government breaks totally with the Quebec tradition while claiming it is simply following up Quebec's demands. They change their goal completely, saying: We separate. Such is our aim. The province of Quebec will never fulfil itself as long as it is not its own master and has full control over its territory, a territory which covers what is now the province of Quebec. Therefore, they change their goal while saying that nothing has changed, and they add to the general confusion on purpose. Indeed, if the Parti Quebecois fosters such confusion among the people, it is because it is up to something. They would have the people believe that they have given up their original option, or at least that it is not as urgent now, and they pretend to negotiate, at times they negotiate and are willing to talk, at other times they withdraw.
A minister makes a statement and a day or two later it is denied or corrected by Rene Levesque himself. From time to time, it is Rene Levesque himself who sends up a trial balloon and one of his ministers, namely, Mr. Morin, tries to catch it back when he realizes that it was not well received by the public. The previous Quebec governments used to demand more autonomy, more specific powers on certain matters, greater financial means to meet their requirements and more scope to set their own priorities.
Such were the demands made by Mr. Levesque's predecessors, but Mr. Levesque does not follow the same line and has definitely broken away with Quebec traditions. On the contrary, he distorts the rules of the game and the image of

Quebec at the negotiating table and at the constitutional conference table.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: It is not a point of order, it is just nonsense!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I think that Mr. Levesque participates in constitutional discussions just for the sake of appearances, which is rather clever, until the situation he manages to create gives him an opportunity to walk out. Then, he will go back to Quebec and say: You see, I tried to negotiate in good faith but it just did not work. I made every effort to reach an agreement with the federal government but it proved impossible.
He is deliberately cheating. And he also impedes progress. This is the most serious problem the federal government is now facing in its constitutional negotiations. He deliberately stands in the way of the negotiating process while denouncing its slow progression. Of course, you can never expect a quick outcome so Mr. Rene Levesque can say: You see it takes too long, it is not possible to come to an understanding, one province wants something and another wants something else. So it is hopeless, the whole procedure is wrong. Then he pretends to take part in discussions so as to be in a position when he can eventually rationalize his unwavering determination to release the province of Quebec from its federal ties.
I believe that Mr. Rene Levesque is too shrewd and so are some of his advisers to burn his bridges in case the referendum he is reluctant to hold on the future of Quebec would not be a success. In this way he could have it both ways. He wants to leave the door open. He was very careful for instance not to take a definite stand with his colleagues from the other provinces. He did not tell them: You know, I have definitely given up the idea of separating Quebec from the rest of the country. To my knowledge he has never said that in federal-provincial conferences. So it is obvious he is playing a game, not a very honest game which is far removed from the political openness which he is bragging about. Throughout his political life he has been saying that politicians must be transparent. Well, he is far from being transparent right now. He is trying to drag us all into his dilemma and confusion. Time has come now-and it is ever more urgent as time goes by-for all politicians to grasp the problem involved, to define the issue at stake, to determine the aims of this country and to come up with a clear question, and for Mr. Rene Levesque-who advocates another alternative-to state what are the advantages and the disadvantages so that the population would be well informed. He should demonstrate how his alternative might be viable and indeed he should show the road to follow. And that is not all. He should tell us exactly how that option can become reality because even though theoretically feasible
January 30, 1979

in practice it will raise a great many problems. He must inform the population about the problems they can expect to face. People must understand the risks involved in that endeavour, the delays inherent in such a process, the unstableness that could follow in Canadian political and social life, particularly in the province of Quebec because finally Quebeckers will have to foot the bill, to restore their social, political and cultural life in a totally modified political context.
I accuse Mr. Levesque of refusing to inform the people. He will agree to consult them only when he is pretty sure that they are so confused by the hotchpotch of words and options that have been proposed that he has a chance of getting a positive answer. What does Mr. Levesque do, talking at length as he does about the true sovereignty of the people? Mr. Speaker, the people are sovereign only when they make their own choices, and especially when they can do so fully informed. Let him give back to the people of Quebec this basic sovereignty which consists in being adequately informed to answer a question which will decide their political future.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we need this referendum legislation so that we can replace the provincial government if it does not hold its referendum as promised. This is a promise that it made to the people in Quebec, but with all the delays, we may wonder whether it will eventually keep its promise. And if the economic and social situations in Quebec continue to deteriorate, will someone not have to act to clarify the situation? And if the Quebec government fails to do so, the federal government needs this political tool which will enable it to consult the people in Quebec about their own future.
It must be kept in mind that we wish Quebec to hold its own referendum. We believe that it is its responsibility; since the Quebec government has brought up the matter of a new option, it must consult the population and we hope that it will hold this referendum. If it does not, however, and if the situation continues to deteriorate, we want to have the means to intervene. Moreover, if the province of Quebec holds its referendum, the question could be so ambiguous that the answer would make no real sense and nobody would know if the people have voted yes or no. This is what happened in the provincial election when the people were told: Vote for us and we shall give you good government and talk about independ-ance later. The people voted on this ambivalent proposal and found themselves with a government which was not satisfied to give them good government-if it is any good-but which also wanted to promote its option of independence for Quebec.
So, if this question is ambiguous, somebody else must be in a position to ask a more precise one to give Quebec citizens the possibility to state clearly what they want and to make a clear choice as to their future. But this is not what is happening and those who are aware of the Parti Quebecois backroom manoeuvres know only too well that since it was elected it has been carrying out surveys on a question and even on several questions. It is testing what the question should be. It attempts to devise what question will bring in the highest percentage of "yes" answers, whatever its degree of clarity. This does not
Referenda
bother them too much. They are trying out questions. And the people are confused and worried. In some cases, and I have seen examples of it recently, a certain anxiety starts to show up. Not so long ago, I paid a visit to a group of senior citizens of my riding.
I met someone who asked me: But what is going to happen if the referendum is deferred? And suppose it is not held? Here is how she put it to me: If I am against independence, how do I answer? Is this proof enough that people are confused? She knows what she wants, she is against independence, but she said: I will not know what to answer. Well, this shows me just how confused people have become.
I have just said in French, Mr. Speaker, that I met a representative of the senior citizens at a meeting in my constituency. That person exemplified the kind of confusion in which the population finds itself with the kind of publicity and manoeuvres the Parti Quebecois is up to in the province of Quebec. This person came to me and asked me: "If I am against independence, how can I answer the question?" That was enough to give me the message that the population has become extensively confused about what is going on. That person knew what she wanted to say. She wanted to say that she was against independence. With all the questions floating around that might be asked on the referendum, she was afraid she would not be able to answer in conformity with what she believes. That is the kind of confusion that has been systematically created by the Parti Quebecois. It is our duty to do something to help the population see clearly how things should be handled in this kind of situation.
The Parti Quebecois is obviously playing games, camouflaging its real intentions by using words like sovereignty association, which they do not even attempt to define in the course of their speeches. That senior citizen who is somewhat removed from the political scene is understandably in a state of confusion. It is our duty to enlighten such people. However, for someone like the hon. member for Rosedale to be taken in by the kind of ploys used by the Parti Quebecois is not understandable.
The hon. member does not see through the exercise of the conditioning of the people. That forces me to the conclusion that some of the leading members of the opposition are politically naive when as members of this House I would expect that they would be politically grown up. It is inexcusable that politicians would get taken in by this kind of manoeuvring and manipulation. Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to participate in this debate. However, after having sat through it yesterday and today I feel compelled to do so. The word "distort" has been dropped often in this debate by way of an accusation by one or other hon. members on the opposite side. Sitting here listening to the speeches during the parliamentary days since we have been back, the greatest distortions have been coming from the other side.
The hon. lady who just resumed her seat and other members opposite have said that we do not really understand the situation in Quebec. Is it because we do not live there? If that is the case, I can equally say that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) does not understand the Yukon because he does not live there. Nor does he live in the province of Quebec. However, I do not say that. One does not have to live in a province to understand what is going on there, any more than one has to live in another country to understand what is going on in another country. It helps, certainly, but I do not suggest to the hon. lady or to any other member opposite that they do not understand the Yukon because they have not lived there. I have been fortunate enough to live in every province and both territories of Canada, but I do not say I understand the country because of that good fortune.
This distortion has been brought out by each successive speaker on the government side, and at the same time they say they are not using the national unity question as an issue in the forthcoming election campaign. All their speeches have been
January 30, 1979

focused on the question of national unity and very little time has been devoted to the dangers inherent in this bill itself. I might say that the main factor-1 am glad to see the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), I believe it is, in his seat because he served in the last war-that caused me to seek the Conservative party was what happened in this country in 1942; I shall have one or two things to say about that in a moment.
Speaking of distortions, the hon. lady says we are against public referenda in Canada. Yesterday I saw she was in her seat when our leader spoke on the subject and made it clear that we were not against a referendum on the question of unity or any question concerning Quebec. We are not against it at all. But we did make it quite clear-the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) did this yesterday in a very eloquent fashion-that the question should be a specific one and that parliament should decide on that question.
The hon. lady says it is logical to ask Premier Levesque to make his question clear in the referendum, that it is logical we should insist on that clarity so that the people of Quebec will not be confused when they come to vote for or against. I agree. But if it is logical to demand this of Premier Levesque, is it equally logical for us in the opposition to demand that the government make its question equally clear before we are asked to pass judgment upon it? So when the hon. lady and others over there say we are against referenda, that is false; it cannot be dignified by any other description. And when hon. members over there say that because of the dangers we see in this bill, and our position in opposing it, we do not trust the people of Canada-I hear this from the NDP, too-that is equally false. It is simply not so. If it is sensible to hold a referendum on the question of unity then, surely, we should know the question; and that has been the practice on previous occasions in this country when a referendum was held. We say: Bring in a simple bill and write the question into the bill. We want a clear question formulated.
Yesterday the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau)-I believe that was his riding; it was either him or the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette)-spoke on national unity. I sometimes think that members over there, when they are speaking on questions as vital as this one affecting the nation have tunnel-vision which prevents them from seeing the 40 per cent of Canada above the 60th parallel. He said he got angry because we on this side were not concerned about the question of unity. Well, if he experienced anger with respect to the debate which is going on today over unity, imagine my frustration and the frustration of those who live in the Yukon. Here are people fighting to get out of the country and there we are in the Yukon fighting to get in. Does the government of the day hear our pleas? Is there any question of holding a referendum to seek the opinions of those in the Yukon wishing to join confederation? I should say not. Indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) takes exactly the opposite view.
For this reason I was disappointed in the report of the Task Force on National Unity because there was not one single reference in that report to those Canadians in the Yukon, to

those Canadians whom I represent-and I come from the most westerly city in Canada. There is a brief reference to the travels of the task force; they say they travelled from St. John's, Newfoundland to Yellowknife. That is as far as the reference goes. We were not totally absent, though, because the coat of arms of the Yukon was displayed on the front cover of the report. That was some small consolation; we were remembered, somehow, but I do not think it was in the minds of those responsible for compiling that report.
The minister who has just spoken says she cannot understand why we do not accept this legislation. She, and speaker after speaker from the other side, have accused us of opposing everything, making a broad, generalized accusation that we are somehow a party of chronic opposition and chronic filibustering. She has forgotten the pipeline legislation of last year and how, if it were not for this party, that legislation might not even yet have seen the light of day in this House.
They distort not only the position taken by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr.Crombie) and the Leader of the Opposition-that rug has been pulled out from under them, now- but they have tried to make an issue of this reference to negotiating sovereignty association, separatism, or whatever. I might remind them of the remarks made by their own leader as recently as December 20, 1977. They were indignant that we or anyone would even consider negotiating a question of separatism with the people of Quebec, yet in an interview with Bruce Philipps on December 20, 1978, The Prime Minister was asked this question:
But there is no real, legal way to separate, is there, Prime Minister? It is not provided for in any law that I know about.
To which the Prime Minister replied:
No, it is not. That is why there cannot be any unilateral declaration of independence. But in the same way there was no law in Britain permitting any of its colonies to separate. When the reality of a colony no longer wanting to be a part of the British empire arrived, well, the Brits just passed a law. What I am saying basically is that if ever Quebeckers by an overwhelming majority decide they no longer want to be a part of this country then they are going to sit down and negotiate with the rest of the country how they can be kept in.
That was said by the Prime Minister. Yet they are accusing us of somehow bargaining the country away by saying exactly the same thing. Of course, we will talk with the people if the referendum which is to be held, presumably in Quebec, is passed by a majority. It is either that or allow the country to do down the tube, and that is certainly not want I intend to do.
I want to touch on something which is quite important in this debate. The Leader of the Opposition laid out the dangers inherent in this legislation with abundant clarity. I, like others on this side who have expressed opinions, am very disturbed by this legislation. It means the end of responsible government in this country. In a moment or two I am going to quote verbatim the words uttered in the 1942 debate by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). At that time he coined a phrase: "Not government by legislation, but government by plebiscite". That is the direction we will take if this referendum bill is passed.

What the hon. member for Gloucester neglected to point out yesterday and what the hon. member for York East neglected to point out, when they accused the Leader of the Opposition of not having read the bill and when they trotted out the safeguards they thought were contained in the bill so that no abuses could occur, was the fact that if this bill is passed, it will permit the cabinet to frame questions, and it will permit the government with its majority-and this legislation is more likely to be abused by the present majority than by any other political party I can think of-to lay on the whips and ask questions regardless of the opinion of anyone else in this House. I have in my hand a copy of the bill. Why does it not incorporate the question to be asked of the people? This bill as placed before parliament will have but one result. It will change the constitutional history of this dominion, in that it will permit the Prime Minister at any time from this day on to submit a plebiscite on any matter whatsoever to the people of Canada, with the authority of this parliament.
That is precisely what we are being asked to do today.
It is so worded, Mr. Speaker, that it is operative beyond the war. It is so worded that the Prime Minister can continue to submit plebiscites at any time and without restriction. Let me ask this question. Why was not the method followed this time similar to that adopted in submitting the plebiscite of 1898? In my opinion this bill represents a milestone along the way that will destroy responsible government. The Prime Minister has said in effect that a great harm was done to the principle of responsible government in 1940 when he promised that there would never be conscription for overseas service, and now in effect wishes to undo the harm so that responsible government may be restored again.
That was from page 835. At page 836, drawing a distinction between the 1898 legislation and the 1942 legislation, the right hon. member said, and I quote:
To illustrate the difference I should point out that under the measure as it now appears before parliament, the Prime Minister and his government do not have to submit any questions to the people, whereas under the plebiscite of 1898 the question to be asked was in the statute. They may place a plebiscite on any question before the people at any time in the future. There is no control whatsoever .. .
When the statute was passed in 1898 there was nothing evasive in the attitude of the government. The question was put in the statute. The regulations as to voting were contained in the statute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I take part in this debate which is of great importance and which will mark an altogether significant step in our collective and political life. Let us not kid ourselves, the sole reason why this bill is before us is the victory of the Parti Quebecois on November 15, 1976. While this bill concerns every Canadian, it is of special concern to Quebeckers for they will have to take a decision on the constitutional future of Quebec.
Quebec is like a giant who has just woken up, a province which now entertains doubts about its history, its culture, its social organization and its political institutions, wondering as well why it should belong in Canada such as it was established in 1867 by the Fathers of Confederation. Yes, Mr. Speaker, Quebec has woken up and possibly this awakening will bring a second breath, a new vigour to the idea of a real Canadian confederation. If members of the Canadian federation want to keep Quebec in, they will have to accept it as a fascinating and full-fledged society.
Referenda
The Task Force on Canadian Unity has just published its report, where it talks, of this awakening, in the chapter intituled The Anatomy of Conflict. It says, and I quote:
For the longest part of Quebec's history one theme dominated the cultural life of the collectivity. That theme was survivance, or sheer survival. This overriding concern for the maintenance of the way of life of a people coloured the relationship between Quebeckers and their compatriots.
But, Mr. Speaker, only an insensitive observer of the life of the province could fail to note a substantial shift in approach in which that community's concern for survival is now expressed by the thoroughly contemporary and dynamic pursuit of its own development.
Mr. Speaker, those remarks were made by a task force which was created by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself and which described itself as being federalist. Such a quotation is a good illustration of the confusion which prevails in Canada today and of the long way we have to go if we are to restore national harmony. The Task Force on Canadian Unity proposes a new federation, and even though Quebeckers feel that those recommendations do not go far enough, yet these reflect a state of mind which is more conciliatory and not based on childish fights. One cannot talk, Mr. Speaker, of that state of mind which is suggested by the task force without wondering about the federal government's state of mind when it comes up with this bill concerning the holding of a referendum on matters relating to the Constitution of Canada.
When I talk about the federal government's state of mind, I refer to its real intentions in relation to the possible holding of that referendum. In any case, if this bill is passed, hon. members of this House may not have to wait long before they get into a debate on a referendum question. This bill does not concern Quebec alone, but the federal government might indeed use it in any litigious matters between the central government and the provinces.
In spite of the constitutional conferences, the present frame of mind is much more directed toward confrontation than toward dialogue. All this is understandable since one side wants sovereignty association and the other seeks centralized federalism. Canada needs a constitutional readjustment and this is the spirit which should prevail. Since 1945, provincial responsibilities have kept increasing. Just think about the importance of natural resources, education, public health. And yet the flexibility of the British North America Act is often limited in terms of subsidies to the provinces.
Always in the same spirit, the election of the PQ is a reaction to an old constitutional arrangement which goes back as far as 1867 and which does not reflect today's reality. I sincerely think, Mr. Speaker, that we shall have to renegotiate seriously the Canadian confederation before holding a national referendum. Otherwise we would be putting the cart before the horse. Can we demonstrate our seriousness to the Canadian people when there were no serious negotiations? I shall accept a national referendum when we have had serious negotiations

January 30, 1979
Referenda
and when the Canadian people as a whole, and particularly the people of Quebec, have before them really concrete proposals.
Assuredly, Mr. Speaker, the Parti Quebecois government is going to hold a referendum within one year; it will seek approval to negotiate the conditions of sovereignty association; this is not a good deal for the federal government and it would be most unfortunate if Quebec should separate from Canada. It does not mean however that the central government should not reform the constitution to make it more favourable to the well-being of Quebec and other Canadian provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to warn the government that its lack of responsibility as far as national unity is concerned could turn out to be very expensive for Canadians. Indeed, by acting in an obstinate fashion, the federal government would help considerably the all-out supporters of separatism in Quebec. In the present context, Bill C-9 would betray the interests of Canadians and provide a dangerous opportunity for propaganda. We have heard about national unity for several years, especially since November 15, 1976. I consider that this word, Mr. Speaker, is mere propaganda because it assumes uniformity and thus does not correspond to the Canadian reality.
Canadian unity does not exist and has never existed, because there have been too many different groups. However, there are groups in Canada that are willing to share their common interests. The central government's role is to channel the common forces in the best interests of all communities. I should like to remind hon. members that national unity implies cultural homogeneity and sometimes a Unitarian government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, such is not the case in our country.
Before asking Quebeckers whether or not they are in favour of sovereignty association or whether they prefer our present federalism, it would be in the interest of the central government to make serious proposals instead of minor reforms such as those proposed in the former Bill C-60. Canada has to be rebuilt in order that our ten provinces and our two territories may fight for a common cause. I believe Canada must form a marriage of convenience, and if this country is to grow, it is essential. All parties concerned should be able to fulfil themselves. There cannot be a really viable Canada and a legitimate partnership unless the two contracting parties have freely agreed to it and unless each party recognizes that it is clearly in its interest to share its existence with others.
Until such time as circumstances change, any partnership such as Canada must recognize the right of all parties to the contract to very flexible formulas for amending its constitution. After 110 years, each and every one of the provinces has the right to examine its situation in relation to confederation and to renegotiate sections of the constitutional act. To date, the Quebec government alone has expressed its intention of holding a referendum on the constitution.

I therefore ask the federal government and hon. members to respect the spirit of the Canadian confederation and wait for the results of the Quebec referendum. I feel that Canadians must express their views on the constitutional future of the country after a provincial referendum. Provincial governments and many Canadian citizens are displeased with the present federal system. The current distribution of responsibilities between the federal and provincial governments no longer reflects reality. The federal government machine has become too cumbersome and we have to submit to regulations that border on inefficiency.
I have here in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a letter from a citizen who lives in Radisson, on James Bay, and who is having problems with the unemployment insurance system. I would like to repeat to hon. members some of his quite enlightening comments about the present system. Here is what he says:
Why should I be against federalism? Perhaps because I am now convinced that I am supporting a costly, ineffective, system which is so overburdened with legislation, regulations, paper work and bureaucrats that it cannot deliver the opportunities promised when I adhered to the system.
Why should I be unable to obtain benefits for which I have been paying premiums for years?
Is it unreasonable to believe that the part I play in a project as remote as James Bay will make me lose the benefits to which I am entitled?
As it can be seen, this citizen is not pleased with the government and he is not alone. In closing he writes, and I quote:
To relieve you from the painful task of reading my indignant comments, I will tell you, sir, that I want to be a positive asset in a Canadian and Quebec community, but if a referendum is to be held in the near future I will not consider it as a political but rather as a practical matter, to wit, have I paid to support a system which has not given me what I could rightly expect?
Mr. Speaker, that is the fundamental question we must answer when we consider this legislation. That is the question the Pepin-Robarts commission attempted to answer. That is also the question the various governments and especially the federal government must answer. That is the question the provincial governments must discuss and it is the issue to which will relate the reforms they will submit to their people.
Mr. Speaker, I insist on the fact that the federal government is a creature of the provinces and that all constitutional reform proposals must come from them. The latest constitutional conferences have indicated a general dissatisfaction which is not peculiar to Quebec. All you can hear about in the province of Quebec is dissatisfaction. The people of that province have elected a government whose option is sovereignty. I think the situation is serious enough and that there is no need for us to make it worse by holding a second referendum without any previous negotiation. I deplore that atmosphere of confrontation which opposes the federal government and the government of Quebec. We have had a war of statistics and we shall soon have a war of referenda.
Mr. Speaker, earlier I referred to the state of mind of this government. I am afraid that its attitude and that of the right
January 30, 1979

hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) are not very conciliatory. On the one hand he wants to adopt this bill with a certain measure of haste; on the other hand, at his press conference last Friday, he refused to acknowledge the Canadian duality which Quebec exemplifies. Something which the Pepin-Robarts commission has already acknowledged. The right hon. Prime Minister has often stated that he would refuse to negotiate the possibility of sovereignty association in case Quebeckers replied affirmatively to the Parti Quebecois referendum. I suggest that the attitude of the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues is quite arbitrary. It is not certain that Quebeckers will reply affirmatively to this referendum. As elected members of the Canadian public, we are not asking the government to negotiate the independence of the province of Quebec, but instead a constitutional arrangement which would recognize the particular character of each Canadian province.
Many recognize that the present government is suffering from a superiority complex, and also from what I would call a chronic case of inflexibility. It is indeed showing its inflexibility by engaging in this all-out fight, when the interests of all concerned would dictate co-operation and understanding between partners. In any event, Mr. Speaker, the present political climate and the general purport of Bill C-9 lead me to believe that this referendum will be a propaganda tool rather than a means of discussion and information. The government restricts the scope of its referenda solely to constitutional issues. Besides setting limits of referendum expenses, the bill defines eligibility to the referendum vote and air time allocated to opposing groups as well as to federal and provincial parties. To go back on those main themes, I must say that I deplore the fact that the bill is concerned only with constitutional issues, whereas several other points could be considered, such as abortion, capital punishment, social policies, and so on.
On December 12 last, the former minister of state for federal-provincial relations and the leader of the New Democratic Party praised the democratic merits of referenda. We even heard the leader of the New Democratic Party give his support to this bill. I would suggest to him that he think it over carefully before voting for this bill. I would like to remind hon. members of this House that the result of the referendum would not in any way compel the government to respect the opinion expressed by the public; so one may wonder what the government's reaction would be to a positive response of the people concerning sovereignty association for Quebec. Once again, the Prime Minister said last Friday that he would not negotiate. This means that the government might follow the policy established before the referendum in spite of the opinion expressed. If the referendum is negative, there will be no problems for the federal government, but we must question the legal value of a strictly consultative referendum.
Furthermore, we do not know the wording or the scope of the referendum question. I fear a serious confrontation might be brought about by two referenda, one by Quebec and the
Referenda
other by the federal government, for each of them will try to rally the people to its cause. Mr. Speaker, I would also like to make a few comments on the air time and the expenses allowed. We can see that the air time will be in part allotted to the federal parties and in part to the provincial parties of each province. This means that the federalist parties will get almost all the air time.
I would also like to voice serious reservations about allowable expenses. Bill C-9 is much less restrictive than the Quebec law. Referendum expenses and contributions made by a person, a group or a political party must not exceed $5,000. But only registered political parties and referendum committees will be allowed to make contributions and expenses exceeding $5,000. I believe that this part of the bill discriminates against small political parties and referendum groups. I cannot see how the government can claim it is exercising democracy with such rules. It becomes very obvious that groups and parties with unlimited funds at their disposal will enjoy a clear advantage over the others and this constitutes a propaganda risk.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my speech by putting hon. members and Canadians on guard against the risk of manipulation of public opinion. I am not imputing wrong intentions to the government, but I do want to warn them that this legislation could be a major asset in the constitutional dispute. Before holding a referendum, it would be preferable that the governments negotiate and put before the people a real common constitutional project aimed at the development of all Canadians and the economic, social, political and human progress of this country. Canada is a great country of which we must be proud. There should be no room here for discord, so let us show the entire world that we are a nation that is basing its relations on mutual respect and harmony.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased for various reasons to be able to enter the debate this afternoon on Bill C-9, the referendum bill. From the outset I had made up my mind that I wanted to take part in the discussion because I believe in this country, Mr. Speaker. I believe in the rights, freedoms and privileges of each group and of each region. I believe that as Canadians we have an obligation to each other, a responsibility to each other, to keep this country united. This country was born as a result of people coming here for various reasons in their search for freedom and opportunity. I believe it is the responsibility of the government to see that those freedoms and privileges are protected.
Canada is made up of diverse groups of people of various cultures and traditions and, indeed, with two official languages, yet it is rooted in many other languages. These rights and privileges have been recognized by this government, but now there appears to be a threat. Indeed, there not only appears to be but there is a threat. One government in this

January 30, 1979
Referenda
country has as its aim to separate from confederation, not necessarily by the will of the people within that province. It has taken upon itself to make that move supposedly in the interest of that region.
The federal government has a responsibility to see that those people get a fair hearing, that the views of those people are respected, that their views are not distorted but are taken into consideration. It is for these reasons that I support this bill.
While the leaders in that particular province have taken upon themselves to move the province out of confederation- and it may even be by various and devious means-they have suggested that when all else fails, as when the support of the people failed prior to the election of 1976, they would not separate from the rest of Canada without a referendum. Subsequent to that many statements were made because it was felt that they did not have the support of the people. When we question the motives and methods that may be imposed upon the people of Quebec we must also take a stand to protect the rights of the people in that province as well as the rights of all regions of Canada.
Many words were uttered in this House in the few days before the Christmas recess on this subject. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) referred to what he called the distortion of this bill by various speakers. I cannot accept that kind of remark, Mr. Speaker, because I am convinced that all parliamentarians are here to represent the views of the people in their constituencies as well as the views of Canadians from all corners of the country. I do not believe for one moment that there are members of this House who would willingly distort the intent of that bill, the words contained therein, or the purpose of the bill.
The hon. member also suggested that the bill was bad, dangerous and explosive. I take the opposite view, Mr. Speaker. The bill is not dangerous, nor is it explosive. The bill is in the hands of the government, in the hands of this House, in the hands of parliamentarians; if it is dangerous and explosive then maybe the hon. member for the Yukon ought to look at himself and his own motives in reflecting on the bill.
Parliamentarians need to take a rational approach. At times in this House we take a very partisan approach, and I have been party to that course myself sometimes in an insignificant way. I do not believe that at this time, however, there is room for partisan politics because the future of this country is at stake. I am convinced that we are all concerned about it. We need to have a unified approach. Goodness knows we have enough discord in various parts of Canada. I even see the discord and fracture on the other side of the House when I hear some members talk about sovereignty association and negotiations for sovereignty association. Then later I hear remarks from speakers on the other side who would not negotiate.
We need to get our act together, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members on the opposite side need to take a look at where they are going. Maybe they ought to consult with their leader and with

their constituents a little more. In the end it will be the Canadian people who will speak. It is at this time and with this bill that the federal government is prepared to consult the people of Canada. It is because of the importance of this issue, the opinions that have been expressed and the hazards that we face that I can support this kind of a view and this kind of an attitude.
I am not even sure what some hon. members on the opposite side of the House are speaking about when they talk in terms of negotiation of national sovereignty. Where is their mandate? They do not have a mandate to speak about national sovereignty or to negotiate with the PQ.
For the first time in history Canada is facing a challenge, the very outcome of which threatens to sever the bridge of her nationhood. It is that important. It is a serious question. Circumstances facing Canadians are peculiar and unprecedented in our history. We are sailing into uncharted waters never before explored. We have a provincial government that is dedicated to separation regardless of what it says. Never before has a government sought a mandate to extricate itself from the bonds of Canadian unity.

speechtext:
that Bill C-208, to amend the Railway Act (ownership of land where line abandoned), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reasons for presenting this bill have not changed since I first introduced it in the House some four years ago. We have discussed the bill and my motion that the government introduce such a bill on at least three occasions. Even though Liberal members, at the urging of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), talked out the bill and my motion, I find that they have not put forward any valid reason for rejecting the bill. While talking out my bill, government members wasted valuable hours by discussing other phases of transportation.
On February 28, 1978, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) spoke for almost 20 minutes on the Hall commission report with respect to prairie grain transportation before telling us that the Minister of Transport had signed an agreement with CNR and CPR in the fall of 1977 which would parallel the intent of my bill. At that time I had not seen the agreement. Since then I have tried to obtain a copy from the minister's office.
Finally I obtained a copy from the office of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowksi) after he was promised one by the minister at a committee meeting. I do not know at this time whether this agreement was signed or not, for I was not able to obtain a signed copy. Whether it has been signed or whether it has been used, no one seems to know. It is very easy for the minister to show a copy of an agreement that he and his department have dreamed up but is it valid? Has it been used? What use has been made of it?
January 30, 1979

For the record, I would like to read a copy of the agreement. It is between Her Majesty the Queen in right of Canada and the Canadian National Railway and Canadian Pacific Limited. It reads:
Whereas CN and CP have been requested by Her Majesty to make a gift, in the public interest, of certain branch line rights of way and they have acquiesced in this request as hereinafter recorded,
Now Therefore the agreement witnesseth that the parties hereto mutually agree as follows:
Upon receipt of an order from the Canadian Transport Commission authorizing abandonement of rail lines within the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta on or subsequent to August 5th, 1977, CN or CP, as the case may be, will forthwith transfer to Her Majesty by way of gift all its title and interest, mines and minerals excepted, to its right-of-way and lands appurtenant thereto. In respect of such line, excepting only the portion of any such rights of way and lands lying within an urban area, subject to the right of CN or CP, as the case may be, within eight months after the date of the order from the Canadian Transport Commission or the date of the abandonment specified in such order or the date of this agreement, whichever is the later, to enter onto such transferred lands to remove rails, ties and other railway materials therefrom. CN or CP, as the case may be, shall be responsible for the payment of taxes and maintenance of such transferred lands until it has removed the aforesaid rails, ties and other railway materials therefrom. General descriptions of the lands which it is contemplated are to be transferred pursuant to this paragraph have been prepared by CN and CP and are attached hereto as schedules A and B respectively and proper land descriptions of these lands will be incorporated by CN and CP in the transfer documents.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF the parties hereto have executed this agreement by their proper officers in their behalf duly authorized in that behalf on the day and year first above written.
I believe this makes it clear that contrary to the statement by the member from Assiniboia the agreement will not serve the intent of my bill. I would, therefore, specifically urge the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Bat-tleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac), who tried to explain that the purpose of the bill was served by this agreement, as well as all hon. members, to read my bill and the agreement. 1 am sure that after reading my bill and the agreement they will see the intent of my bill is not reflected in the prairie rail agreement.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, the agreement between Her Majesty the Queen in right of Canada and the CNR-CPR, is for specific rail lines abandoned in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. This is a real issue. This agreement is not for all of Canada, it is just for the prairies, and not necessarily for all lines that may be abandoned in the prairies. This type of agreement should be included in a bill and included among federal statutes, not decided through ad hoc agreements, secret meetings and agreements within agreements.
Agreements of this type apply only to specified parts of the country, leaving other parts of the country to fend for themselves. For example, British Columbia is excluded from the agreement. There are problems in B.C. of equal if not more consequence, when it comes to rail abandonment. Agreements such as the one to which I referred forget an important concept-the retention of rail corridors.
The requirements of British Columbia, because of their dwindling rail system, are of at least equal importance as those of the prairies. This can also be said for eastern Canada and
Railway Rights of Way
the Atlantic provinces. My bill would have the effect of ensuring that important rail corridors will remain open and of giving federal and provincial governments responsibility for these corridors which they will have to assume in the future.
The responsibility to provide transportation corridors in the future, when our present non-renewable fossil fuels run out, will fall on the government, not on the railway companies. It is true the companies may have had to pay for some land in the past, but this was more than compensated for by the many "sweetheart" deals they received from the government in the form of land grants and subsidies.
I take exception to the idea that the railways should retain the rights to the mines and minerals. They were granted land for the purpose of building a transportation system. It adds to the credibility of the claim that CPR is no longer simply a transportation system but is, rather, a huge conglomerate with various other interests. Imagine the confusion which would result if a mineral find should occur on a narrow corridor while these big conglomerates are holding the rights. Surely the Minister of Transport, the Department of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission can see far enough into the future to avoid this type of situation. It may only be a rare event, but think of the confusion it would cause.
A most important aspect of the agreement, Mr. Speaker, is the exclusion of portions of land and rights of way that lie within an urban area. This is one of my main arguments for having such a bill on the statute books. If valuable national assets are permitted to be broken up and sold off for short term advantage, future generations will be deprived of vital transportation corridors.
In the long run, shortage of renewable fuels will enhance rail transportation using these corridors. As fossil fuels are depleted these rail corridors will become increasingly important. The expense of reacquiring abandoned rights of way or opening new ones in built-up urban areas will add significantly and unnecessarily to transportation costs. It is in these very areas, urban areas, that it is most important that the corridors revert to the Crown.
No wonder, Mr. Speaker, the railways were so fast to sign the agreement, if the agreement has, in fact, been signed I have seen no evidence that it has. It is no wonder they made this agreement with the Minister of Transport. They knew full well that they were trading off less expensive land in rural areas in return for very expensive land in urban areas and cities.
Let us consider, for instance, Penticton, British Columbia, where a portion of the CPR's line has already been the subject of a hearing for abandonment. Marathon Realty is not too interested in the rambling line through the mountains, but even before the rail line abandonment is final it has already begun to sell off and take options on valuable property in the city of Penticton, some of it on the waterfront.
It is something again to know that a cattle rancher in a rural area has experienced a hassle in getting a crossing over a CPR

January 30, 1979
Railway Rights of Way
line which has not been used for years, yet when he travels to Penticton he can see that rail crossings have already been paved over, knowing that approval for abandonment has not yet been granted. This is a typical way in which the railway tries to use its "authority".
My bill says that title of ownership should be vested in the Crown in the right of Canada. This, of course, means that the federal government would obtain ownership.
I know that there is some concern among the provinces that they should be the ones to receive title. I am not arguing against that, as I believe they have a good case. After all, in most cases Crown land is owned by the provinces. During the hearings of the constitution committee last year it was determined that both federal and provincial governments could own Crown land. This point could be sorted out at the committee level, should the government in all seriousness see fit to pass this bill at second reading. It might be best to have these rail lines revert to the Crown in the name of provincial governments. After all, the provinces should be the ones to deal with municipalities, not the federal Minister of Transport, who says he wants to. An appropriate amendment to this effect could be made in committee before the bill is brought back for third reading.
What kind of heritage are we going to leave our children and grandchildren? They are the ones who will have to pick up the pieces and pay the costs if we in this day and age do not protect their rights.
The CPR and the CNR are big corporations. The CPR has branched out in many ways. When one looks at its record over the last few years, one wonders whether it cares about transportation. It would appear that the government-controlled CNR is more concerned about trying to emulate the CPR than about transportation in Canada. The railway companies are oriented to the bottom line of profits. They do not care who gets hurt.
It is the responsibility of the CTC to look after people's interests. Therefore, at committee hearings and at hearings with regard to the Carmi railway abandonment my appeals to the commission were to ensure that the interests of our children and grandchildren are protected in the future. I believe the CTC has the obligation to come to parliament with recommendations to change rules or laws which do not offer this safeguard to their heritage.
Parliament has an obligation to protect the heritage of future generations. It is for this reason that I have introduced this bill. Special agreements will not solve the problem. I know my bill can. When railways are granted permission to abandon lines anywhere in Canada, the rail rights of way should revert to the Crown.
The government should take its responsibilities seriously. The Minister of Transport must be aware of this and should not send in his troops to talk out the bill. He must not become a pawn of the railways. In the interests of our children and grandchildren he should support my bill or, failing that, introduce a government bill to the same effect.

It is time for the government to be as tough on railways who rush to abandon rail lines as it so generously supported them years ago when rail lines were first constructed in this country.
