speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-208 is one which my friend, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker), has proposed before in this House, and it has been debated on other occasions. Having said that, I do not mean to imply that it should not be debated again, because such debate serves to give the hon. member and all members of the House an opportunity to look again at developments, happenings, activities and at the rationalization of the branch line network in western Canada. This debate affords us an opportunity to review some of those things.
I was pleased to note that this afternoon the hon. member put forward some additional arguments-I think they were very sound-to support the suggestion that the bill should be considered, even though certain other events which the hon. member discussed and which I will be discussing have taken place since the time he first proposed the bill and since the time this bill was put forward in the House.
It is interesting to look over the past record of this bill and other questions relating to railroad rights of way. This bill once again illustrates the schizophrenia of the position of my hon. friends opposite. The hon. member who proposed this bill suggests that rights of way from abandoned railway lines should be turned back to the federal Crown. I believe it was on December 19, 1977 that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), who was in the House a few moments ago, seconded by my good neighbour to the west, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), moved, and I quote:
That the Minister of Transport notify western provincial governments that he is prepared to immediately negotiate with them and with the railroads to ensure that ownership of abandoned rail line rights of way be under provincial jurisdiction.
So two completely opposite proposals have come from our hon. friends opposite within the space of about a year. However, we are getting accustomed to that. We have seen this approach in other areas as well, I suppose the most recent one being the one which has been referred to in debates and exchanges in this House over the last few days, and that is the turnaround of the official opposition with regard to economic policy. After berating this government over the last several years for the amount of government spending and the level of the deficit, over the holidays the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) showed us that he is not really worried about the deficit. Indeed, the Leader of the Opposition would enlarge the deficit and spend his way back to prosperity, after spending a number of years telling us to contain government spending and so forth. I mention this to indicate that this kind of schizophrenia in Tory policy has become the custom around here rather than the exception.
I recognize that the bill proposed today by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary represents a very sincere effort and that in fact to a large degree it is presently part of this government's initiatives with respect to dealing with branch line rights of way. The government and particularly the Minis-
January 30, 1979

ter of Transport (Mr. Lang) have moved much further than the hon. member suggests in his bill. The bill suggests that rights of way should revert to the federal Crown. The hon. member gave a number of very valid reasons why that should be the case. This government and transport people have said that we should go further than that. Rights of way should go to the federal Crown, but in the case of prairie branch lines the rights of way left as a result of abandonment should go directly to the rural municipalities involved and, in most cases, from them to adjacent land owners.
I think we are making very good progress on the whole question of what to do with the rights of way of these branch lines and of making sure that we are getting the land back into the hands of municipalities and from there to its rightful owners.
During the recent Christmas recess, I met with a number of different groups and individuals in my constituency. Among those groups were rural municipal councils. Some of them were municipalities which had branch lines within their boundaries which were scheduled for rebuilding, retention and reconstruction. Also, some of them were municipalities which had branch lines in the process of being abandoned. The following questions came up at different council meetings: what is happening in this regard, what is the government doing, what can they do, and so on.
The steps respecting the abandonment of branch lines in the prairie network are as follows. First, there is a Canadian Transport Commission order authorizing the abandonment of a particular line. Second, under the agreement between transport, the CNR and the CPR, which was spelled out by the hon. member who introduced the bill, the land is deeded from either of the involved railroads to the federal Crown. Third, as I understand it, the titles could well contain leases or other related caveats as they are transferred. Fourth, the land then is dealt with by a railroad bed steering committee, with the object of getting the land back into the hands of the party who deserves it. Fifth, in most cases the level of government best able to decide and to deal with it certainly will be the rural municipality. It goes without saying that in most cases the individual or person who will have the opportunity to acquire the land will be the landowner or the ratepayer who owns land on either side of the right-of-way. Quite often railroad rights of way cut through crop land, pasture land or whatever.
Much has been made of the Hall commission. Other spokesmen have indicated that ownership of rights of way should go back to rural municipalities, so that they in turn can sell them to the rightful parties in order to compensate them in some manner for the loss of tax revenue, which revenue resulted from rail lines going through municipalities. I suspect there will be more red tape for the municipalities than there will be financial revenue from much of the land. This is because it is not worth a great deal to the municipalities in that sense, nor to the landowners whose land was split or divided by rights of way. I do not see a great deal of revenue accruing to the
Railway Rights of Way
municipalities, even though it will be of some assistance and some value.
Initially the provincial governments of the prairie provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba were very, very upset about the notion contained in the bill put forward by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. They were upset about the idea that this land should revert to the federal Crown and not to the provincial Crown for whatever reason. I have yet to find any validity or common sense in the arguments put forward by the provinces. I suppose it is a classic case of how far provincial power advocates will go in attempting to make the case that they will fight with the municipalities and the adjacent landowners over the right to have the land in their hands, leaving the federal Crown out of it entirely.
It has been a realization for me as to how ridiculous two levels of government can become when attempting to establish their rights in this regard. It is all right for the federal government to put up hundreds of millions of dollars to rebuild railroads, for subsidies and everything else; but when it comes time to accept back the land from the railroads, suddenly that particular aspect of railroad activity becomes a provincial responsibility and is no longer the right of the federal government.
Some of that antagonism seems to be waning. The province of Saskatchewan is represented on the committee to deal with farmers, rural and urban municipalities. The committee will look at the entire process of determining who should be the rightful owners of some of the land being turned back.
A great deal of progress has been made since the hon. member put forward his bill. I recognize his bill goes further than the present practice and policy of the government, although the practice and agreement established by the government and the two railroads to deal with the rights of way, which are now in the process of being abandoned across the prairies, certainly will form a precedent for rights of way in the hon. member's part of the country and other parts of Canada. As I said on a previous occasion in this debate, the bill does not go nearly as far as the government has gone in dealing with this question. The bill is somewhat redundant because we have progressed beyond the point referred to, the objective of the hon. member's bill.

Railway Rights of Way
I have a copy of the report entitled: "Grain and Rail in Western Canada", written by Mr. Hall, commonly known as the Hall report. At page 103 he made comments regarding what should happen to the railbeds once rail lines are abandoned. He indicated that the land should go to the provincial Crown, and that the provinces and municipalities should make a decision on what happens to the land. Referring to page 103, in part it reads as follows:
We propose to forestall controversy by providing that, upon abandonment, the roadbed-that part of the property abandoned represented by land-vest in the provincial Crown for disposition as may be mutually agreed to between the relevant province and municipal authorities.
Mr. Hall goes on to make a few more detailed comments as to why that decision should be made between the involved province and municipalities.
I should like to make a few comments on why railway lines should not be abandoned. Of course, I realize that some lines must be abandoned, but when one refers to the abandonment of lines, one should also talk about why some lines should not be abandoned. 1 see the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary agreeing with me. At the present time, this issue is a very big and controversial one on the prairies.
About two weeks ago the minister released a report from the Prairie Rail Action Committee which studied some 2,400 miles of rail line on the prairies. It recommended that about 60 per cent of those rail lines be abandoned.
I want to go back over a little bit of the history of rail line abandonment. I know the minister has said that upwards of 70 per cent of rail lines on the prairies are preserved in that they are in the basic network and will be upgraded. That is excellent, but I think a number of rail lines that have been abandoned in the past, and a number of rail lines the government now proposes to abandon, should not be abandoned.
The PRAC report refers to 2,400 miles of line of which 60 per cent should be abandoned. It is our position and the position of the wheat pools, and they are tremendously credible as they are the ones who built the elevators and deliver 70 per cent of the grain in the province of Saskatchewan, and nearly as much in Manitoba and Alberta, that most of these lines should not be abandoned but should be preserved and upgraded, to the benefit of the people who live in the area.
Let me point out to the House what it means to some of these communities to lose their rail line. First of all, the lines that PRAC studied are the lines that in respect of which Hall could not really make a decision. Hall looked at about 6,000 miles of rail line and said about 2,000 miles were utilized to the extent that they should be put immediately into the basic rail network. He said that an additional 2,000 miles of line were not being used enough, that there were too many inefficiencies and it would cost too much to upgrade them. He suggested that they were not worth-while and should be abandoned. Those rail lines have now been abandoned by the government. The bill before the House has no direct relevance to those lines as they have already been abandoned.

Mr. Hall had a third category in respect of which he said further study was needed. He recommended the setting up of a prairie rail authority to study these lines and make recommendations to the government as to what should be done. Instead of that, the minister set up the Prairie Rail Action Committee which has advised him to get rid of 60 per cent of those lines in respect of which Mr. Hall could make no decision.
What we have said, and what has been said by the wheat pools and the province of Saskatchewan, and many other agriculturalists, is that 90 per cent of those lines should be preserved. We have suggested that they are used to haul a sufficient amount of grain to warrant their upgrading. We have said they serve a sufficient number of farmers and, in many cases, the towns rely on them, and that their removal would cause inconvenience for a lot of people. We have suggested that the farmers who haul grain to the elevators on these lines would be greatly inconvenienced if the lines were removed.
Let me point out four things it would mean to the people if the rail lines were abandoned. First of all, it would mean an extra haul to the farmers. Instead of having to haul for seven or eight miles it would mean a haul of 20, 30 or even more miles. Secondly, it would probably mean an increase in provincial and municipal taxes to upgrade the roads the farmers would be using to truck their grain instead of moving it by rail. It would also mean the speeding up of the demise of the small farm because it is only the operators of large farms who are economically able to truck the grain this extra distance.
The abandonment of a line would also mean the end of those towns on the line because the farmers are not going to go to those towns when they haul their grain to other towns. Since they haul the grain to other towns they will do their shopping there. If the farmers shop in those towns it is those towns which will prosper and grow. These other small towns will gradually diminish and die. We have had many studies which indicate that when a rail line is abandoned about half the businesses in the area eventually go. Many of the people who would normally retire and move to those towns will eventually move to other towns on an operating rail line because they want to retire in a place that is booming and growing.

Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity on other occasions to join with the hon. gentleman across the way who proposes this bill this afternoon in discussing the question of rail line abandonment and the disposition of railway rights of way following any abandon-
Railway Rights of Way
ment procedure that might take place. I remember a day in the House of Commons just about a year ago when this subject was debated by my hon. friend from British Columbia and a number of others of us who are very interested in this matter. I am pleased that the hon. member has taken the initiative once again to bring this issue to the floor of the House, because it is a matter of importance.
Those of us who have spoken since he introduced the bill just happen to be western Canadians, all three of us from the prairie region. Hon. members will understand the interest and concern we have for this subject because of the important job that must be done and is now being done in western Canada to rebuild the grain handling and transportation system across the prairies and to export positions. It is a vital industry for our region and for Canada. There is not a more positive element in our national balance of trade figures than the figures relating to grain exports. Therefore the questions of how we can best take advantage of our grain exporting opportunities, develop markets, produce the grain to satisfy those markets, and then efficiently transport that grain to the markets, are important questions for all Canadians.
Once again I commend the hon. member for raising this issue in the House of Commons as he has done on other occasions, and I hope our discussion this afternoon will serve generally to bring matters up to date as to where we stand at the present time in this regard.
The bill proposes an amendment to the Railway Act which, on the surface, appears to be relatively straightforward. The proposal can even be considered to have some considerable merit, although the sincerity of the opposition in giving support to this bill must be questioned when one recalls that on December 19, 1977, a colleague of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) moved, under Standing Order 43, in the House:
That the Minister of Transport notify western provincial governments that he is prepared to immediately negotiate with them and with the railroads to ensure that ownership of abandoned rail line rights of way be under provincial jurisdiction.
If I read the hon. member's bill accurately, I think he is proposing that if there is to be ownership by the Crown, it should be the Crown federal, not the Crown provincial. In the case of the Standing Order 43 motion which was raised on that other occasion-

subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF WAY TO REVERT TO CROWN
speechtext:
I am glad to have that clarification, Mr. Speaker, but I am not sure that it totally disposes of the issue before us. The distinction between ownership by the provincial Crown or federal Crown in some instances is likely to be an important distinction, and if it is something that can be reasoned or rationalized away that easily, perhaps that would be an end to the issue, but I doubt that in the negotiations such a conflict could be resolved that easily.
To listen to some of the spokesmen for the provincial governments in western Canada after the publication of the Hall report, I had the impression that they held this issue very dearly and saw through their eyes that there would be for them some considerable problem if the ownership of these roadbeds were to revert to the Crown federal.
The federal government has taken what I think is an eminently reasonable position, that where a roadbed is eventually abandoned the ownership reverts automatically to the Crown federal but only for the purpose of facilitating the transfer of ownership to the party which should, in the final analysis, hold it permanently. In the case of the roadbeds in the prairie region, the federal government has no vested interest in being the permanent owner of those parcels of land. Rightfully, the ownership should be in the hands of the local municipality or the adjacent farm owner. I think this may be an important point of distinction on this issue raised by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary.
The hon. member's motion, bearing in mind the region from which he comes, is more broadly based and does not simply focus upon the prairie region and the question of grain transportation. I recognize that his intention is to work a broader amendment into the law than that relating simply to grain lines on the prairies. Be that as it may, I think the most crucial and pressing issue in the country today relates to those rail lines in the prairie region, and that is why I think that the comments in this debate since the bill was introduced have focused specifically on the grain transportation question. The federal government recognizes that there is merit in federal Crown ownership of these rights of way, but only for the purpose, as I said before, of ensuring a smooth transfer of these lands to the logical owner who will derive the most benefit from them.
There are, of course, other considerations which must be taken into account with regard to this amendment. The Hall commission report recognized that municipalities affected by rail line abandonment would suffer through a loss in taxation. As a result, the government has made the decision that the disposition of abandoned rights of way on the prairies will be executed in such a fashion as to allow for compensation for that tax loss to accrue to the municipalities, in recognition of the fact that their revenues would be reduced by the loss of the taxes on the roadbeds.
To expedite the transfer of title to the ultimate owners, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) early last fall signed an

agreement under which Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway will transfer to the federal government all roadbed property identified for abandonment in the prairie provinces. As the minister stated before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications last year, this agreement was reached specifically to ensure that the land is transferred to the logical recipient as quickly as possible. There is no intent of retaining the land for the federal Crown, as I have said.
In order to facilitate the process of ownership transfer, and recognizing the need for municipal compensation, the Minister of Transport has established for each of the prairie provinces a rail roadbed steering committee which will determine the disposition of abandoned rights of way in each province. Meetings have already taken place with prairie farm and municipal groups.
I can think of three specific meetings which were concerned with this question and there have undoubtedly been other discussions about it. The rural municipal organizations and the Western Agricultural Conference, which represents most farm groups in western Canada, have given active support to this initiative by the federal government. The municipal associations have now been formally invited to participate in this consultative process, and the prairie governments have also been invited to lend their support to the plan even though, as I said a few moments ago, some of them were reluctant in the first place to get involved in the federal process because they drew a strong distinction between the merits of ownership on the part of the Crown federal and ownership on the part of the Crown provincial. If the interjection from my hon. friend from British Columbia is some indication that the provincial governments have got over their concern about this issue to a certain extent, then I welcome his remarks.
The procedure worked out by federal officials in consultation with western representatives calls for the establishment in each province of a rail roadbed steering committee. This committee will consist of two representatives selected by the rural municipal organization, one from the urban municipal group, one representing the general interests of farmers, one representing the Government of Canada, and one from the provincial government should they agree to participate. I am glad to note that the province of Saskatchewan has agreed to provide a representative, thus giving provincial support to the process. Hopefully the same sort of co-operation will be forthcoming from other prairie governments.
In each case the steering committee will consider all the interests that might be involved in the abandoned rights of way. Although the ultimate owners will primarily be the municipalities and the adjacent farmland owners, exceptions will be allowed. Each proposal will be considered on its own merits.
Again, we might identify a potential problem that could exist in the generalized approach put before us this afternoon by the hon. member who proposed the bill. It might not be
January 30, 1979

possible to adopt a general principle that would apply in each and every case of an abandonment or potential abandonment, in all regions of the country. Even in the case of the prairie region there are different interests expressing a desire ultimately to own the roadbeds that might be involved, and even in a rather homogeneous situation we see different viewpoints and interests being expressed. If there is that much diversity involved in what is a rather self-contained situation on the prairies, it is understandable that if the same principle were to be applied across the country, the numbers of disputes and competing interests would be rather remarkable indeed, and it might not be possible to adopt any legislation of general principle that would be workable. There will always be exceptions, competing interests, and a matter of judgment to be applied in each case as to where the ultimate ownership should fall.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is also involved in the case of those rail lines that happen to pass through Indian lands. The department will have the right of first refusal for any land which passes through Indian reserves in those circumstances.
The steering committees in each province will consider legitimate uses proposed by the provinces, such as transportation and utility corridors, subject, of course, to the payment of appropriate compensation to the affected municipalities. With those two exceptions, the interests of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the interests of the provincial governments, the general principle in the prairie region seems to be that the abandoned rights of way would be offered to the local municipality as a first priority and thereafter to the adjacent landholders who would pay for the land with the payment accruing not to the federal government but to the municipality as a form of compensation for their tax loss.
Earlier I mentioned that meetings of the roadbed steering committees have already been held. In keeping with the government's policy of ensuring that railway lines not required on the prairies revert quickly to those who can make most use of them, in most cases that means primary producers, the memberships of steering committees is oriented to small urban and rural municipality representation. I have already gone over the proposed representation for each of these committees. The membership covers a wide range of interests, and the individual representatives are involved actively in every day prairie life. . It is hoped that these committees will be in a position to proceed quickly with the transfer of these lands. The procedure I have outlined is extremely flexible and adaptable to the specific conditions present when any particular rail line is proposed to be abandoned. This will ensure that these properties are disposed of in the most equitable fashion, bearing in mind all of the potential competing interests that might come to the fore.
While there is merit in the germ of the idea proposed by the hon. member from British Columbia this afternoon, I think that at least in relation to the prairie regions, events have rather overtaken the proposal. We have a procedure in place
Railway Rights of Way
which is dealing with the situation effectively and which seems to have the general support of farm organizations and municipal organizations, and at least the province of Saskatchewan and, we hope, other provincial governments in western Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: The hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty), who was speaking at five o'clock.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my friends on the other side for their kind applause. I hope they will not greet the end of my remarks with the same enthusiasm as the beginning, but I hope hon. members will find my comments both informative and constructive.
Parliament is continuing its debate today on Bill C-9, a bill which the government says will give it a valuable tool for carrying on the fight in favour of national unity in Canada. This bill sets the ground rules whereby the federal government

can hold a referendum on any question relating to Canada's constitution. The powers which the government is asking for are very broad. In the words of the bill itself, it would give the government the power to hold a referendum on:
-any question relating to the Constitution of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada is of sufficient importance to warrant obtaining the opinion of electors on that question-
The referendum could be held in every part of Canada; it could be held in only one province or held in a combination of provinces. Deciding the scope of the referendum, the question to be asked in the referendum and the terms, would be left to the Government of Canada. Once the bill is passed, and it is certain to pass because the NDP have assured the government it will add its support to the government majority all the way down the line in passing this contentious piece of legislation, the government will have the power for five years to hold a vote on any constitutional question whatsoever that it chooses, once it has gone through the procedure of rushing a pro forma motion through this House of Commons. Just to obtain pro forma approval of the House of Commons, which would be gagged after 40 hours' debate on the motion, the bill provides that this government, which has demonstrated its callous disregard for parliament, will simply have to tolerate 40 hours of debate in the House of Commons before the debate comes to an end and it can ruthlessly use its majority to put aside any dissent.
That would be an enormous amount of power to give even to a good government which had proven that it knew how to use power wisely, but in the hands of this government which has ruthlessly undermined the role of parliament and implemented policies which have resulted in deep tears in our national fabric, this amount of power would be intolerable.
The Progressive Conservative party will vote against this bill. We know that in the end the support of the socialists will ensure that the bill will be passed. Fire is an element which can be an extremely useful device. In the hands of careful and responsible people, it can produce tremendous human benefits, great advantages for us all. However, in the hands of the irresponsible it can cause serious property damage. In much the same way public referenda can provide an important and valuable device in our political system. They can ensure a means by which our citizens can make important decisions about the laws under which they live.
My province of Ontario has long had a system of local option which allows residents of local communities to decide whether liquor will be served in public institutions in their community. That is an example of how referenda can be used effectively and for the public good in at least one of the jurisdictions in the country. They have been used well there for years.
Many people have asked that the federal government allow referenda on a broad range of topics in which there is considerable interest. The members of this party are not saying that there are no circumstances under which referenda can be justified, that there are no circumstances under which referen-
January 30, 1979

da would be useful for the Government of Canada. Indeed, several of our own members have proposed specific topics ranging from taxes on one hand to capital punishment on the other where they, as individuals, feel that a public vote would be desirable.
Just yesterday our leader indicated in debate on this bill that if the government had brought in a specific bill with a specific motion in it which could be approved by parliament, dealing with the question of national unity, and if it was clear that a referendum on that topic would be helpful in maintaining the unity of Canada, that sort of bill would have had our support. However, what we in this party are saying is that in a parliamentary system every attempt by a government to hold a referendum that would end up costing the taxpayers millions of dollars directly and indirectly before it was completed should be justified on its own merits.
No government has the right to ask parliament to approve broad legislation requiring only a rubber-stamp approval by the government majority in order to be used. In the hands of an incompetent or irresponsible government, this potentially valuable tool of a referendum could become very destructive indeed.
I ask the government members here tonight this question. If they feel that the voters might be asked a question whose importance is so self-evident that no more than 40 hours of debate would be required, why are they then not prepared to drop this bill and instead bring before parliament a specific bill authorizing a specific resolution or a specific question to be asked? Why did they come to parliament now to get virtual carte blanche for the next five years for whatever course of action they might choose to adopt?
Supporters of the government might argue that a crisis in confederation will develop over the course of the coming months that will make swift action urgent. If that is the case, as the government claimed it was the case when it suspended civil liberties in Canada seven years ago, what political party in this parliament would stand in the way of rapid approval when the time came?
Instead of indicating a respect for our parliamentary system of government, this administration asks us to give it the power now, and to entrust parliament's rights to the government's good will. That is not good enough. Let us take another look at the wording of the bill. It would allow the government to ask for a vote on "any question relating to the Government of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada" which the government would like to see voted upon.
We should look also at the definition in clause 2 where the scope is so broad as to include, and I quote:
-without limiting the meaning of that expression,
(a)	the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada, and
(b)	the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada;
Referenda
The wording of this bill is so broad in its scope that it would give this government virtually unlimited power to ask for a vote of the people on almost any issue it chose, because virtually no issue in Canada could be excluded from that if the government chose to define it in a way which was very broad. There is absolutely nothing in the wording of the bill which would restrict the government from asking about matters that fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Indeed, as recently as yesterday, a government member went on record as saying that is what he saw in this bill. I quote from page 2652 of Hansard when the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) made this statement:
As far as I am concerned, this bill provides for this parliament to determine when or where a referendum should take place, not only on matters of federal jurisdiction but on matters of provincial jurisdiction and concurrent jurisdictions and even in unassigned jurisdictions. That is the way I interpret Bill C-9, and I think the opposition should face up to it.
We do face up to it, Mr. Speaker. It is unfortunate that some members of the government have not been as candid as to the government's intentions when speaking about this bill. They talked about how narrowly it would be confined. The last member who spoke on behalf of the government talked about this referendum we have before us as if he knew what question would be asked. Parliament has not been told what the question is that will be put to the people. We have been given no guarantee that it would be used sparingly, this broad power which the government is seeking. In fact we have been warned of just the opposite by a Liberal member that the government could use this bill to invade areas of provincial jurisdiction.
This bill would empower the government to inflame further the bad feelings that exist between Ottawa and the provinces by invading areas where it has no right to be. Some members opposite were present in Toronto when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke to a Liberal fund-raising dinner one week before Christmas. I read the transcript of the Prime Minister's comments at that dinner. I think it is worth considering part of them in the context of this bill. After a long recital of why he felt his government is indispensable, the Prime Minister turned to the question of resources. These were his words:
You know, we're hearing the provinces say: Well, these resources are mine and the federal government shall have nothing to do with these resources. We don't say that. We say: The resources of any part of Canada belong to Canadians. And sure it means a little bit of hassle, a little bit of confrontation, but not a big one.
What is there in this bill that would prevent the Prime Minister if he wanted "a little hassle" with the oil-producing provinces and decided to hold a referendum on the question of whether the federal government or the provinces would control the reserves? It would be this government that decided to hold the vote in the first place. It would be this government that would decide what wording of the question would be most likely to obtain the preferred result. And it would be this government that would use its majority to authorize the vote only after 40 hours of debate in the House of Commons.
The leader of the NDP says that this bill is an essential tool for the unity of Canada. But what would he say to Allan Blakeney in Saskatchewan if the Prime Minister chose to pit

January 30, 1979
Referenda
the consuming provinces of Canada against the producing provinces? It would be too late then to say that parliament should not have given the government such a broad grant of power.
Just last week the Task Force on National Unity brought down its report. It was clear from the hearings held by the commissioners that one of the major causes of disunity in this country has been the willingness of the federal government to invade areas of provincial jurisdiction. In the words of Premier Robarts at the time, the government forced medicare on the provincial government, to "change the constitution without amending it." This has been the practice of the Liberal government through successive changes in the cabinet.
The bill before us places no restrictions upon the ability of the government to ask any question related to the constitution, whether it deals with an area of federal jurisdiction or not. At the very least, the leader of the NDP could have asked that the government confine the bill to matters either exclusively, or at least partly, falling under federal jurisdiction, before offering his party's wholehearted consent. The unity of Canada requires that much at least as a pre-condition of support for a bill of this kind.
The constitutionality of this bill deserves more than just lip service. And by "constitutionality" I mean more than just the strict legality of the bill itself, because it is probably arguable that any jurisdiction in Canada has the right to poll its constituents on virtually any subject, whether it relates to an area falling under its jurisdiction or not. But surely good constitutional practice requires that the question whether the government is acting in an area in which it has the right to legislate should be considered when a bill of this kind is being brought forward. Otherwise, the whole concept of the distribution of powers in Canada between the federal and provincial governments is made meaningless.
The government attempts to justify the introduction of this bill on the basis that the announced intention of the Levesque government to hold a referendum in Quebec on the question of sovereignty association, whatever that means, makes it necessary for the federal government to have the power to do the same thing. The question that Quebeckers will be asked will be loaded in favour of a positive vote for separation, according to the bill's defenders. And the federal government should have the ability to ask its own question of Quebeckers, or, as the Prime Minister speculated, of the people in the other nine provinces as well.
What surprises and disturbs me, if the future of Canada is to be decided by a succession of referendum battles, first held in the provinces, then held by the federal government, and again, perhaps, in the provinces, is that at no time in the debate on this measure have government speakers addressed themselves to the question whether "sovereignty association" can even be a topic for discussion between the two levels of government.

As my leader has said, if the government had brought in a specific bill to deal with the question of national unity, or specifically dealing with something related to the constitution, we would have been prepared to entertain it. We remain prepared to entertain a bill of that kind. But we are not prepared to grant carte blanche to the government for the taking of a tool which can be used to divide Canadians and to pit region against region. Mr. Speaker, if the federal government can ask a question on the subject of sovereignty association which has any legitimacy, then surely the government has also to accept that the break-up of Canada is a proper topic for debate. And if the federal referendum on Quebec's role in confederation is to have any legitimacy, the federal government must also accept that a provincial referendum on the same subject might have legitimacy too.
By even suggesting that Canada's future should be settled by a battle of referenda, the government gives up its right to say the separatists are unjustified in claiming that a provincial referendum can be the proper expression of the public will. Surely if the government intends to use this device in that way, it owes it to the Canadian people to address itself to that issue first, namely, whether or not the course of action it is proposing will in fact give assistance to the separatists by legitimizing the referendum route they are taking.
All that is left, Mr. Speaker, if we accept the legitimacy of a vote to break up Canada, is whether the question asked was fairly put and whether the results achieved are in our best interests. No one made this argument better than the leader of the New Democratic Party when he spoke in the bill's defence in December. Here are his words, as recorded on page 2044 of Hansard:
No one can pretend that a referendum will be a permanent solution or the only solution. But if you do not believe in violence, if you do not believe in oppression, then surely the people have to be given the right to determine if the possibility of the survival of the country is at stake. That is why I, for one, agree in principle with the means of the Parti Quebecois, which is a democratic means of establishing a referendum although I oppose that party with all the energy, intellectual, moral and physical, within the law that I can muster on their objective.
Listen again, Mr. Speaker, to the operative part of that paragraph. It is this:
... then surely the people have to be given the right to decide if the possibility of the survival of the country is at stake. That is why I, for one, agree in principle with the means of the Parti Quebecois, which is a democratic means of establishing a referendum ...
Those were the words used by the leader of the NDP as he spoke in defence of his party's position on this bill. The leader of the NDP quarrels with the goals of the PQ which are to break up Canada, but he applauds the means they have chosen to do so. Nowhere does he question whether any government has the legitimacy to discuss the break-up of Canada itself, although the referendum would do that. And nowhere does he spell out what he would do.

speechtext: Wrong, wrong!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Read Hansard. You will find it on page 2044 of Hansard. What other construction can be put on his words? As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, my leader made the unqualified statement, which he repeated this week, that our party will not negotiate sovereignty association with the government of Quebec. Surely the people of Canada are entitled to the same assurance from the leader of the NDP and from the leader of the government opposite.
We heard a great noise coming from the government benches earlier. You could see they were uneasy. They had good cause, because they are probably as aware as we on this side of the House of the transcript of the talk between the Prime Minister and Mr. Bruce Phillips of CTV which was taped on Tuesday, December 20, 1977, and shown on CTV National Network on Sunday, January 1, 1978. Let me read the exchange. Perhaps Liberal members opposite will follow me and address themselves to the implications of what the Prime Minister was saying:
Bruce Phillips: But there isn't any real legal way to separate, is there, Prime Minister? It's not provided for in any law that I know about.
Pierre Trudeau: No, it. is not. That is why there cannot be any unilateral declaration of independence. But in the same way there was no law in Britain permitting any of its colonies to separate. When the reality of a colony no longer wanting to be part of the British Empire arrived, well, the Brits just passed a law. Now, you know, what I am saying basically is that if ever Quebeckers by an overwhelming majority decide they no longer want to be part of this country, then they're going to sit down and negotiate with the rest of the country how they can be kept in. What I say at this point is I will not make them change their mind by force of law. I do say that somebody will have to sit down and negotiate with them and it won't be me.
What was he saying? "Somebody will have to sit down with them and negotiate and it won't be me." It won't be the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) either, because if Quebec
Referenda
separates he is going with Quebec. He would choose it over Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the leaders of both the New Democratic Party and the Liberal party have a responsibility to the Canadian people to come clean with this House and to indicate on what terms they are prepared to talk about the break-up of Canada. That's the common thread which runs through those two quotations I read to the House.
Mr. Speaker, the crisis in our confederation today is grave but it is not unique. I tried to correct an hon. member opposite when he said earlier that this was the first time a provincial administration had attempted to destroy Canada. That's not so. Joseph Howe stood for office and won a strong mandate on a platform of pulling his province out of Canada. Some people argued then that Macdonald should support a policy of asking Nova Scotia to give the new country a fair trial for a year or two and then to make up its mind about what it wanted to do, but Macdonald's response was unequivocal, unlike the response of this government and that of the New Democratic Party. It was this:
That, it seems to me, would be giving up on the whole question. The ground upon which the Unionists must stand is that repeal is not even a matter of discussion. I hope that the Colonial Office will be firm in this matter. If the Duke of Buckingham says at once to Howe and his confreres that they have nothing to hope or expect from the British government, 1 think the matter will end there; but if he should be weak enough to say "You should give this system a fair trial for a year or two," the consequence will be that the professional agitators will keep up the agitation for a year or two and then will return to the Colonial Office and plead their own factious course and its success as an evidence of the persistent refusal of the people to be incorporated in the union.
Macdonald's response was blunt. Repeal, he said, was not a matter of discussion. I and hon. members on this side of the House do not deny that the nature of the threat posed to confederation by Joseph Howe was different from the nature of the threat posed today by Rene Levesque, but Howe's challenge to our national survival was every bit as real as Levesque's is today. The future of Canada as a nation was considerably less secure in 1868 and in the years immediately following confederation than it is today.
The courses of action which are open to this parliament today remain essentially the same as they were in Macdonald's day. We can either state without equivocation that Canada is indivisible, or we can decide to haggle over the terms. There is no third option.
Where we in this House should be turning our attention is to attacking the reason why growing numbers of Canadians throughout this country are giving up on Canada. We should be looking for ways of proving to them that we understand their concerns and problems, and that the federal government, instead of increasing the tensions between different parts of the country, will work to eliminate them.
In 11 years this government has taken a centennial spirit for this country's future and replaced it with bitterness between French and English, between producer and consumer, between government and the private sector, between the provinces and

Ottawa, and between east and west. As testimony at the hearings of the Task Force on National Unity demonstrated, virtually every measure, without exception, taken by the government in the name of national unity has further embittered Canadians over the course of the last 11 years. That is the legacy of 11 years of the Trudeau government.
What is worse is that the government has cynically used national divisions, which deepened as a result of its policy, for partisan ends. On virtually every platform-and we have seen it here in the course of debates in the House-from which a Liberal speaker talks, whether it be the Prime Minister or the lowliest Liberal backbencher, the issue of national unity is used in a pitch for votes, as we saw today.
Perhaps the most cynical version of this ploy is the claim that if Canadians decide that they are fed up with 11 years of arrogance and incompetence on the part of this government and vote to throw this government out, they will be spelling the end of Canada because Quebeckers will feel that the rest of Canada has somehow turned its back on them. We have all heard that claim by the Liberal party throughout Canada.
If it is true that in this bill, or in the unlamented constitutional proposals which died an early death last fall when even the government's supporters in the Senate turned on it, the government has armed itself with the weapons it needs to defeat the separatist challenge, then we must ask ourselves why all the other solutions to the problem that the government has presented over the past 11 years have failed.
To listen to the government talk about how it has discovered the key to national unity in Canada is to forget who was in power a little over two years ago when Rene Levesque swept to office in Quebec. What has happened since that time to make the government's claims more credible, when less than a year before the election of the Parti Quebecois the Prime Minister announced to Canadians that "separatism is dead in Quebec"? The legacy of this government's term in office is that our country is more divided today than it has ever been before in my lifetime, and yet the government continues to exploit our national divisions for partisan gain.
Let us turn for a minute to the question of whether a federal referendum throughout Canada following a PQ success in Quebec would truly promote national unity. First, it is unclear whether the government would feel bound by the results of a referendum it held any more than the Laurier government felt bound by the results of Canada's first referendum.
The explanatory package which accompanies this bill states that the government could choose to consider itself bound, but in leading off in this debate in December the Minister of Justice stated at least twice that the government could simply disregard the results of a vote if it disagreed with them. It is worth reminding hon. members of the remarks of the minister when he was questioned by one of my colleagues to the left.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the interpretation in the latter part of the hon. member's question is the proper one. The referenda under this bill will be purely consultative, and there is no action required by parliament or by any legislature following any particular result of any referendum.
The minister said later:
I reiterate that it is clearly a consultative process. There is nothing in the Constitution of Canada at the present time that could make the result of a referendum binding on the government, parliament or any particular legislature.
What the minister said was that this government is prepared to go ahead, hold a vote, spend millions of dollars of taxpayers' money, allow passions on both sides of an issue to be inflamed across Canada, see the results come in, and then-disregard them if the government chooses to do so. No other construction could be put on the minister's words. The government could say, "We appreciate hearing from you, but we did not like the answer you gave, so we are going to ignore it." That is what the government calls direct democracy. The hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) said essentially the same things in his remarks last Friday.
Let us imagine for a minute what would be the state of national unity in Canada if the government said it had found a constitutional issue which was so pressing that it should be put to the people in a nationwide vote and then, after millions of tax dollars had been spent and Canadians had expressed themselves on the issue, the government announced that the people had voted the wrong way and that the government would not support them. The vote would have been nothing more than a costly public opinion poll which wasted the time of the electorate.
Let us consider another possible scenario. The most recent Gallup poll on the question shows that support for Quebec's separation today is stronger in English Canada than it is in Quebec. Let us assume that the government decided to hold a national referendum designed to allow the rest of Canada to show Quebeckers that they were truly wanted. What would be the result if, in the middle of the campaign, an emotional issue such as the question of bilingual air traffic control were to crop up? What would happen if Rene Levesque, intent on provoking a backlash in the rest of Canada which would permit him to claim that the country wanted to be rid of Quebec, were to introduce legislation in the Quebec National Assembly to strip away the rights of the English-speaking minority? Can the government say, in confidence, that English-speaking Canadians would be immune to that bait?
Finally, let me deal briefly with one of the assumptions in this bill which is supported both by the government and by the New Democratic Party, namely, that it is improper for the public to vote in referenda on non-constitutional issues but that questions related to the constitution lend themselves equally well to popular votes. Pointing out that a number of my party's members have called for a referendum on capital punishment but are opposed to this bill, the leader of the New Democratic Party said, "You can't have it both ways." What he did not explain is how he can have it both ways.
January 30, 1979

I say to the bill's supporters that unlike a referendum on such issues as capital punishment, abortion or taxation, which tend to cut evenly across demographic and geographic lines, the referenda which will be authorized by this bill would tend to divide Canadians along the lines of our deepest historic divisions. They will polarize Canadians on the basis of language and region.
I do not know how, in the name of national unity, the bill's supporters can say that they would refuse to allow Canadians to be heard on the questions which the polls show they would most like to have a vote about, but would encourage referenda to be held on the questions most likely to ignite bitterness between the language groups or between regions. It just does not make sense. This is the constant theme we have seen running through the arguments made by the government, that its goal is to let the people decide, to have democracy in Canada and to give the people a chance to be heard, but Gallup conducted a poll asking what issues Canadians would be most interested in having referenda on if they felt that referenda were justified. The results of this poll were released on Saturday, December 9, 1978. It found the following:
When Canadians, 18 years and over, were asked, in October, whether they would favour or oppose a referendum on capital punishment, 82 per cent replied affirmatively. In March of this year, when this question was first put to the Canadian electorate, exactly the same proportion favoured a referendum.
That is an issue which the government says-perhaps with justification-should not be put to a vote. I do not know; that is an issue for debate on another day.
The report continues as follows:
Questioned further on what other issues might best be settled by referenda, the majority could think of none-68 per cent. The most frequently mentioned issue was that of Quebec separation-12 per cent-
I hope the minister is listening to this. The issue of Quebec separation was followed by his bill. The report continues:
-followed by constitutional changes-3 per cent-
That is the public demand to which this minister is responding. What sort of mockery is it when the government creates a charade of pretending to be in favour of public input and participation, but it says that that participation can be only on issues about which it wants to hear from the public, and not on the ones about which the public wants to talk to the government? What sort of hypocrisy is it when the government comes before parliament with this type of bill and says that it will authorize votes in areas where there is not strong public demand, and denies Canadians the right to be heard on other issues about which they are concerned? What sort of hypocrisy is it when the government then says that, even if there is a vote, it may well choose to ignore Canadians afterwards? How will the government explain that after the vote has taken place?
There has been a constant thread running through the debate concerning the role of referenda in a parliamentary democracy. The hon. member for York East stated his views on it in the House yesterday. He felt that many of the British
Referenda
institutions embedded in our constitution were not sufficiently modern or up to date to serve present needs. He indicated that they had to be brought up to date, and that perhaps the various traditional ways in which we have operated in Canada just are not operating properly any more. The hon. member said that the entire British concept of a parliamentary sovereignty is a matter about which we should ask questions. It is worth taking a look at the hon. member's particular comments. As reported at page 2650 of Hansard, the hon. member said the following:
The classic "responsible government" approach is becoming tougher to defend in twentieth century society, not only in Canada but also in Great Britain. Those who are quick to bark on the other side should look at what is happening on the other side of the pond in relation to what is happening to responsible government, aside from all their labour troubles. They should pay attention to what is happening in a constitutional sense in Great Britain, the mother of parliamentary democracy.
The hon. member continued his speech by indicating that he strongly supported the bill, and that he felt it would be an advance for our system of democracy in Canada. As reported at page 2651, the hon. member said the following:
The Tories say "no" for consulting the people by means of a referendum; or if you want to use another phrase, by direct democracy.
This was the theme of his speech. I think it would be useful to go back to the last time when parliament was torn apart by a debate on the role of referenda in Canada. It would be useful to look at what the authorities had to say at that time about their role in relation to the parliamentary system. I found one government member who said the following:
The popular view in my constituency and the Toronto area in general is to put the question of capital punishment to a national referendum. This would certainly mean rule by the people in the literal sense; but the passions of the people run high. For me, the spectre of the disorder on the streets of Paris in 1792-94 develops in the scenario of a nation governed by referenda.
Countries that revert to putting questions to referenda often find that more problems are created than are solved. The Canadian referendum of 1944 on the conscription issue intensified racial and regional opinion and created tremendous difficulties, difficulties which were only spared the government by the conclusion of the war. The same analogy may be drawn with the 1975 United Kingdom referendum on the European Common Market, and the recent Italian referenda on divorce and abortion. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it could be argued that the results of the recent Italian referenda have helped to destroy the unity of the Christian Democratic party and precipitated the present political instability in Italy.
Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) I will take my chances with the theory of representation as clearly enunciated by Mr. Edmund Burke, and followed by many politicians in this House and the British House over the past 200 years.
Who was it who said that less than two years ago? It was the same hon. member for York East who spoke yesterday.

It would be a disaster for the country if the Liberal party were allowed to say that one's opposition or one's being in favour of this bill meant that one was any more or less a Canadian. Quite frankly, I am tired of listening to members on both sides of the House saying, "I am a better Canadian than you are because I have been somewhere you have not been, or I have fought somewhere you have not fought." We should be well beyond that kind of argument and feeling in this House. It was Adlai Stevenson who said that partriotism of that kind is the last refuge of scoundrels.
The unfortunate tragedy and political difficulty facing the country today is threefold. First, neither the New Democratic Party nor the Conservative party have an effective electoral presence in the province of Quebec. It is an obvious fact, but frequently we are too embarrassed to state it. I state it frankly, but not with any great pride. Our country and the province of Quebec would be politically much healthier and saner if there were a federal opposition presence in that province. Another sad fact is that the Liberal party has no federal presence in western Canada and a declining federal presence in the province of Ontario. That is a tragedy for the country as well. The

third great tragedy is that in November, 1976, the only means by which the people of Quebec could express their fatigue and dislike of the corruption of the Liberal government in that province was to vote for the Parti Quebecois.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I speak for myself, and I am sure for many members of this party, when I say I approach the question of referendums with no great enthusiasm. If this were a normal time in the course of our history, and we were not faced with a constitutional crisis, I would have neither truck nor trade with referendums, and 1 am sure nobody in our party would either. I will say quite clearly why. I think the drawbacks of referendums in general have been described well, if a little unfairly, by my colleague, the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty). They were described yesterday in the speech by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark). In my view the greatest protection and the greatest presence the people can have in a democracy are the election of members through a strong party system, members of conscience who are prepared to take their position on matters of conscience to the people as individuals, and decide on matters of party politics as members of a political party, to be elected or defeated on those decisions. Neither election nor defeat is a disaster, and it is not the worst thing in the world to be defeated. It is a function of a member of parliament to reflect, to consider, to weigh, to debate in caucus and to rely on party judgment, his own judgment and on the opinions of his constituents, and then make up his mind accordingly. As I say, in a normal constitutional time that would be the course I would adopt, and I am sure it would be the course that would be adopted by members of this party. The fact is that in November of 1976, for the reasons I have described and not because the people of Quebec in 1976 were voting for separatism, a party which is committed to the breaking up of the Canadian federation was elected to form a government. The fact remains that there has been an election in Quebec that has had a dramatic effect on the constitutional situation in this country. The impact, the desires and the aims of the Premier of Quebec have never been sufficiently understood, appreciated, and realized by the Conservative party. If members of that party had realized them, I do not think they would have been able to take the position they have taken in respect of the bill which is before us at the present time. Nor would they have been able to say the things that many of their leading members have said about Mr. Levesque and his real aims and desires, and the desires and aims of his party.
Let me say to the hon. member for Rosedaie (Mr. Crombie) that I saw the CTV interview program, as I am sure many people did. I am not challenging for a moment the hon. member's love for Canada or his faith in Canada. That would be absurd. I have known him too long and too well for that. However, I think he has made a fundamental mistake in his assessment of the aims of Mr. Levesque, and a fundamental mistake in looking at the national unity question in this country. That is a question of judgment. To say simply that Mr. Levesque wants a settlement with honour is a mistake, as it would be a mistake to say that it would be more difficult to negotiate with Mr. Ryan, the leader of the Liberal party in Quebec who is, whatever else, a federalist, than with Mr. Levesque. To talk about the two as if you were talking about the same game betrays an ignorance about the state of the country that is profound.
I think we are entitled to ask the same question about the Leader of the Opposition. That hon. gentleman has stated very often that he is prepared to be flexible, to negotiate, and to talk. He has said most of our constitutional problems have been created by the arrogant attitude of the federal government, and we must have discussion and words; we have to reason together and we must adopt the model of the Kingston conference, where they had five Tory premiers together in Kingston, for the protection of the confederation and for the purpose of discussions with Mr. Levesque. That is his serious assumption of the threat that is presented by Mr. Levesque.
I am not suggesting that national unity and leadership are the only issues facing us, but I am saying that the people of Canada will be asking themselves if this is the leader they want to have negotiate with that very tough set of cookies in the province of Quebec, particularly if that is the assumption he makes of Mr. Levesque's intentions.
I did not create that issue, Mr. Speaker. The Government of Canada did not create that issue. The Liberal party did not create that issue, although I understand it is going to make it an issue. I am afraid the Leader of the Opposition has made it an issue by his attitude.
The second thing which changes my mind about referen-dums is not solely related to the province of Quebec, and not solely related to Mr. Levesque and the election of the Parti

Quebecois. The second thing is the fact that we are now embarked at last, thank goodness-out of a sense of crisis but also, I hope, from a sense of common purpose and achievement-on a path of constitutional reform. We are looking at a very different set of institutions and relationships between the federal and provincial governments, and between the House of Commons and whatever second chamber we decide to create. All of these changes will take place within the tradition of common law and loyalty to the monarchy, which are not in question. It would be absurd to suggest they are in question. Nevertheless, there are some very real institutional changes that will be going on, and I think this is a very healthy thing.
We have a Senate which I have called in the past "the indoor relief department of the Liberal party." It performs no real constructive or useful function in the federal system. It does not do the job which a second chamber could really perform in a federal system, and it is ridiculous that we have been so long in reforming that institution. We have a House of Commons which, as I suggested in my earlier remarks, has a party system that at the moment does not reflect the reality of representation in Canada. It is not true to say that there are no New Democrats or Conservatives in Quebec, because there are. It is not true that there are no Liberals in Alberta, because there are. There is no reason why-and I say this as a member of a parliamentary party which has been consistently under-represented in this House since it was founded over 40 years ago, not in terms of talent but certainly in terms of numbers-we are not entitled to look at the possibility of a reformed electoral system as well as a reformed second chamber. Even in such an instance there is still the question of division of powers. It is a difficult and exciting question and has been raised once again with the Pepin-Robarts commission report on national unity.
I must say in answer to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo that I do not believe that all of the wisdom in Canada rests with the provincial governments. I do not believe that when Premier Lougheed and Premier Davis get together and come up with an idea, that that is all there is to be said about the future of Canada. I believe that Canada is a bigger, better, and greater place then all of its parts put together, and that is the function of the federal government.

This cannot be done simply through a series of conferences between the premiers and federal government officers.
I tried to get into the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa in October, just after I was elected. I could not even get in, and 1 am a member of parliament. The man on the street in Broadview, walking down the Danforth does not know a thing about the Canadian constitution, but one thing he does know is that before he is from Broadview, Toronto, or Ontario, he is from Canada. We are in the process, and we may not even know or realize it-and some of us are so far behind the times we do not recognize it-of creating a new nationalism and a new nationality.

The outstanding thing about that conference was that these people, wherever they came from- and we all came from somewhere-
