The commitment which we all had at that conference and the admission was that we did not want to be known as Greek, Italian, Barbadian, Anglo, Irish or anything else, but as Canadians. These leaders were looking to the federal government for a new constitution that would protect their mul-ticulturalism and social rights, and some of them even wanted us to protect their linguistic rights. The point is that they did not want to go to Bill Davis, Peter Lougheed or the provincial governments for the protection of their new sense of nationality, citizenship or pride in Canada; they were looking to the
[Mr. Rae.)
federal government for it. For any party to ignore that sense of nationalism and not see that nationalism as a tremendous source of strength which needs to be mobilized toward a new consensus, is to be blind to the future of the country, and is simply looking at old patterns and old divisions.
I would like to look now at some of the criticisms which have been made against this bill. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has said that the government was spreading disunity, that instead of fighting fire with fire it was fighting fire with gasoline, that it was a blatant attempt to subvert and undermine the responsibilities of the Canadian system of responsible government. She said that it was a complete departure from parliamentary practice, and that the scope of the legislation was so broad, so large, and so wide that it presented a threat to the civil liberties of every Canadian. She also said that it amounted to a complete departure from the freedoms which we have valued in the common law for centuries.
In looking at this bill realistically, I do not see those dangers there. There are problems in the bill and I have severe reservations about certain aspects of it, but the principle of saying to the federal government that there is no right in a federal parliament to hold a referendum on the constitutional future of Canada, at a time when we are faced with a constitutional referendum in the province of Quebec and when people are crying out for constitutional change because they want to be proud members of a new country, is simply nonsense and, furthermore, political suicide in the province of Quebec. I do not come from the province of Quebec, but the one thing which has impressed me is that every single member from Quebec, with the exception of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), has spoken in favour of this bill. They have said, "Please give us this bill; do not leave us in the hands of a provincial government which is determined to load the dice and stack the decks," to use the words of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.
I think it is worth remembering that there are interests in the province of Quebec which may need to be protected by the means we are giving the federal government and the federal parliament at this time. I put it as tentatively as that. I am not an enthusiast on the subject of referenda, and I have indicated my reasons. If these were normal times I would not be in favour of a referendum. The question raised is whether, when we know there is a government in Quebec which is soliciting political support with every means at hand, we want to say to the federal government, "You have no means; you cannot do it; we are not going to let you do it."
The hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo asked why we do not come here with a specific question. Mr. Speaker, if I were playing poker with Rene Levesque I would not want to put my money behind the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo-I can tell you that! He would walk in and say, "Here are my cards; what have you got?" That is not the way the game is played; this is a tough
January 30, 1979

game, and we do not know what the question put by Rene Levesque will be.
Already reporters are asking what we are going to do if Rene Levesque wins the referendum, and if we are going to negotiate with him. I reply that I am not going to answer that question. I am not going to deal with the question. Do those reporters ask Rene Levesque what he is going to do if he loses the referendum-if he is going to negotiate with the federal government? Of course they do not. They know he is a serious politician. I would ask that the federal government be as serious in the defence of federalism as he is in the pursuit of independence.
The Leader of the Opposition paraded all the horrors-that we could have a referendum on any subject-that it would change the Constitution of Canada-that it would change the law of Canada-would threaten the Indian minorities, the Inuit and the blacks-all the minorities and every group. That is what I call parading the horrors. It is an example of exaggerated fantasy as a result of a kind of paranoiac thinking which comes from being in opposition so long.
The fact of the matter is that there is one minority in Canada now which is seriously under threat. I am sorry to say that happens to be the English language and the immigrant minorities in the province of Quebec. That is the reality. It is not the fantasy. It is not the fantasy of looking at all the things the Liberals could do if they went collectively bonkers and if the opposition went home for five weeks and the Canadian people took leave of their senses. The reality we are looking at is what is going on in Quebec today. That is the crisis; that is the difficulty; that is the situation we have to meet. I say that we are entitled to ask that the official opposition be as serious, as tough-minded, as clever, and have as great a sense of the whole of the country as we ask of the government when we criticize them for being so inadequate.
Where did Roncarelli come when his liquor licence was cut off by Maurice Duplessis? He came to the Supreme Court of Canada, and won his case because he had federal rights and was able to come to the federal government to have them protected. Where did the people who suffered under the padlock law in Quebec come when they could not go to the provincial government-when these tremendous provinces had the Duplessis's, the George Drews, these great protectors of civil liberties-where did they come? To the Supreme Court of Canada.
The fact is that when minorities are under threat we should look at the reality of the situation and at what is really happening. Let us deal with the crisis that is facing Canada now, not some fictitious crisis the opposition is creating because of its generalized fear that the government is going to make national unity an election issue. That is what we are facing at the present time. I think the concerns of the opposition can really be met by looking at what this legislation does, and I will express my criticisms of the legislation as I consider this point.
First of all, the referendum question provided under this bill has to deal with the constitution. It cannot deal with every
Referenda
subject under the sun, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday. It has to deal with the constitution and that is what this debate is about-the Constitution of Canada-constitutional reform. That is what Pepin-Robarts is all about; that is what Rene Levesque is all about; that is the subject of today's discussion. The question has to be limited to that.
This matter is going to be debated in this House. I think the 40-hour limit is ridiculous, although it is more extensive than it looks at first blush. It is about three weeks of debate. I think the limit should be taken away to satisfy our concerns on this side of the House that the matter is going to be thoroughly debated.
The question would be put to the people; it would be discussed and debated. There is protection in terms of all political parties and registered groups having access to the CRTC rules and so on. It is much more liberal and free than the position that has been put forward by the Parti Quebecois in the province of Quebec.
The answer to the question or set of questions would be consultative. People keep asking, "What if he asks a question about Indian rights?" The answer is simple. What happens? Nothing. There is the Supreme Court, the BNA Act, the constitution, the common law-those things will not suddenly be dissolved by the holding of a referendum. This bill does not provide for that and it is absurd to suggest that it does. It shows a fundamental misunderstanding of the realities of political life. It would not lead to a unilateral change and it cannot, because of the nature of our political system.
If the government were foolish enough to hold a referendum in the province of Saskatchewan on the question of natural resources, the results would be disastrous for it. They would lose their referendum. We would clobber them, Mr. Speaker. I have a little more faith in the common sense and intelligence of the Canadian people than some members to my right seem to have. I do not think the Liberals are able to brainwash completely and dominate the people of Canada or Quebec so that the people would not give a reasonably intelligent answer to a reasonably intelligent question on the matter of the constitution.
I should like to end my remarks with a quotation from "Essays on the Constitution" by Frank R. Scott. At page 372 he wrote:
A combination of forces-military, political, and economic-made it possible to find a common ground for the original constitution one hundred years ago. We seem to be at the stage that Canadians had reached just before the BNA Act was adopted.
He commented that we must not think we can be exempt in Canada from the creative force of nationalism in our own country. Then he went on to say:
Nehru once said that there is a good form of nationalism, and a bad form of nationalism; the good form is that inherent desire in man to live in a society that enables him to express himself to the fullest; the bad form is the rigid application of racist doctrines that can lead to disaster. Both the good and the bad forms of nationalism are usually to be found simultaneously in any nationalist movement, and the question is, which one will prevail? The answer to that depends on many factors-

He further commented:
A frustrated nationalism turns to primitive weapons, just as a frustrated individual may seek release in a primitive nationalism. On the other hand, a strong sense of national identity can be a protection against the crushing conformity toward which technology is constantly driving us.
It seems to me that is the heart of the issue-Whether we are intent in Canada, including Quebec, in creating a new national identity with new national, economic and social institutions that deal proudly and effectively with the problems that face all Canadians, or whether we are prepared to be locked in, hindered by the mind-set and institutions that have in some way blocked the aspirations of the people of Quebec and also the aspirations of a great many other Canadians as well, those for example, in Toronto, in Newfoundland, in the Northwest Territories, in the west, in fact everywhere.
I think that a referendum, while not critical or most important, is a useful mechanism, a useful device in the mobilization of that political consensus. It is not a tool that I am particularly fond of in general political terms, but in the specific political situation that we are faced with today, in the crisis of Quebec and in the crisis of confederation which we face, it could be a vital tool in seeing that federalism is presented fairly, fully, generously, and with the decency and dignity we all want to see it presented in the province of Quebec. I have no faith that the Liberals will do it on their own. As I said before, I have no doubt that if this government, and when this government, is thrown out, there will be other parties to take their place that will be able to govern Canada. Canada is bigger and stronger than the Liberal party. If there are other parties that take this government's place, I want to see a referendum as a mechanism in their armoury as well. It is not a partisan political thing. It is not something to do with the survival of the Liberal party, but obviously that is an aspect of every piece of legislation that comes in here.
Sometimes we have to step back from our narrow armies that we come from and ask ourselves, "What is the crisis of Canada", "what is the crisis of confederation", and what are the mechanisms and the political means that we can use to create something different, something new and something exciting? I say two cheers for referendums. It is not the best mechanism nor is it the only mechanism. But it is not a threat to our liberties, it is not a threat to this institution if it is only consultative. It is not a threat to ourselves if we have the confidence, the ability and the strength to use it in the best interests of people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be briefer than those of some of the previous speakers who indulged in a lot of verbosity, but I will endeavour to be frank and sincere, and I hope that I will not duplicate any remarks that have already been made.
Bill C-9 which we are debating this evening says that it might be cited as the Canada Referendum Act. It is entitled

"An act respecting Public Referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada." Quite frankly, I have nothing against plebiscites and referendums or going to the public generally under certain circumstances. 1 am sure that many members of parliament and other Canadians will agree with me on this. Despite the proposals that have been presented to us within the last 12 months by the government on constitutional reform, and also despite the existing situation in Quebec, one must look at this bill for what it is or is not and for what it is worth.
I understand that in some countries in the Commonwealth, referendums are held with respect to the adoption of amendments to their constitutions or on constitutional problems or questions. However, it should be pointed out that such referendums are held after full debates on the specific questions are conducted in the legislatures or parliaments concerned. Plebiscites are held sombrely and soberly on the questions concerned. Amendments of constitutions then become subject to the approval of the electorate. This is done after unlimited debates in the parliaments or legislatures on the specific questions which are to be put to the people.
Bill C-9 proposes just the opposite. It is a piece of legislation which would allow a campaign, similar to an election campaign, and even the implications of the Canada Elections Act of this country, which result in a great deal of expense to the ordinary Canadian through taxes, tax exemptions and income tax. This bill would put political parties and politicians to work to create greater adversity and hatred over what should be a serious, fundamental and sombre constitutional matter. To make things even more ridiculous, the results of a referendum under Bill C-9 would not even be conclusive or binding upon parliament or the electorate. Bill C-9 is unfair and undemocratic because of its numerous provisions permitting the implementation of regulations by orders in council. This is a dictatorial and improper procedure.
When we are dealing with people's rights at the constitutional level we should not permit the cabinet or a deputy minister, who turns out to be some bureaucrat, to issue orders in council or regulations. That is what parliament is supposed to be all about. We should be here to halt and restrain the issuance of decrees, edicts and regulations. In view of the fact that constitutional questions are basic and fundamental problems, fundamental to the rights and privileges of each and every Canadian, a bill which proposes the matters implied in this bill-and there are several-must not provide for orders in council or regulations.
When the bill comes before us for approval or disapproval, it should contain a specific question. It should contain those matters which are to be changed in the constitution, or any amendment. It must set out the full details of a proposed question or constitutional amendement. For example, if Canada wants to adopt the constitutional amendment act which was presented last spring by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), then such a bill should be presented first for unlimited debate, but every clause in that bill should be presented. If there is a question to be referred to the people, then that
January 30, 1979

question should be so stated in the bill. It should be presented to the people after an unlimited debate has taken place in this forum. Certainly it should not be held at the time of an election.
Furthermore, on any question in a debate of this kind there must be-and this should be pointed out clearly-no guillotine or closure procedures. Specifically, constitutional questions and amendments in any event must be debated without limitation in the House. To be effective they should be presented to the people for approval. If they are not approved by the people, then the statute or question would not become effective.
If the government continues to follow what in the past has been its usual arrogant and ill-conceived procedures, then this bill would prove to be yet another weapon or instrument of separation and division in the country. I am reminded of such items as the B and B Commission report, the Official Languages Act, its improper and costly implementation, and the national task force on Canadian unity report. The list goes on and on. All these items should have been or should be shelved. Referendum, hatred, division, separation, an aura of suspicion and infection are arising from the government benches. It is to be regretted that this has been orchestrated in the emotionalism and steam already prevalent through political motivation.
One need only read the legislation to see that, like a number of other bills presented in past years, it is a horrid piece of legislation. If such a bill were to be presented it should have been presented long ago, certainly long before November, 1976.
Implementation of this bill is likely to be the last straw for Canadians. It is likely to break the Canadian back. It is certainly an example of the government's lack of confidence and faith in Canada and its people. It is also an example of the government's knowledge of the people's lack of confidence and faith in this government.
It is my sincere hope and prayer that the government will review this legislation again, review it carefully, and withdraw it at this time. Quite frankly, I have glad hopes in the future of Canada. I only hope and pray that governments and politicians will refrain from pouring their distasteful and far too potent and volatile fuels upon an already fragile situation.
Surely this government should know what happens when the wrong paths are taken, and many they have taken. Look at the economic and unemployment situation caused in large part by the many errors in judgment of this government, errors resulting in government waste, and errors in government spending caused by government instability.
It may not have been intentional, but throughout this debate there have been references to Rene Levesque. Frankly, I do not see this as a positive way of achieving national unity. It is undoubtedly putting Canada and parliament on the defensive. This is very poor strategy. Let us get back to economic issues and sensible issues, issues that will help put bread and butter on the table of the ordinary citizen.
Referenda
My plea to this government is to withdraw this bill immediately before this country is completely destroyed by an instrument of destruction. We do not need another instrument of destruction such as Bill C-9.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me on this very important bill, I should say on this major weapon which is Bill C-9. Indeed, the government wants to arm itself in anticipation of a fight over the results of the Quebec referendum. Even if this bill has been introduced because of the referendum campaign that has already been launched in Quebec, it remains, Mr. Speaker, that every democracy can provide for the need to consult the people directly at some time on a certain issue. Consequently, such an eventuality must be considered and, for this reason, the government is justified to propose a legislative framework for such population consultations. Please note that I said the government is justified, because if this bill had been introduced, say, a year or two before the 1976 events, our reaction would have been different.
But under present circumstances I have some reservations, some doubts about the motives for introducing this bill.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, the short-term objective of this bill is merely to provide a weapon against the referendum law of Quebec. That is why, I imagine, the government chose to restrict it to constitutional matters. Clause 2 defines those constitutional matters as "the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada, and the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada".
The referendum is a health tool; by that I mean that, to my mind, a referendum is a healthy tool for a healthy democracy; and it is only fair for the people to be consulted about its fate. However, what really concerns me deeply is the use that might at times be made of that tool, in this instance the referendum.
This bill authorizes the federal government to organize a referendum in one or several provinces of Canada. In a way this piece of legislation could become an instrument by which the federal government could force a decision on the elected government of a province through a referendum. We should keep in mind that Canada is a federation of states. Therefore it would not be a good sign to see the federal government go over the head of a province because the latter disagrees on a given point. I am not referring here to the particular situation of Quebec, I am speaking in a general context. We should keep in mind that the provinces have elected parliaments which have
80047-32'/2

clear jurisdictions and which represent directly the people; it is with them that the federal government should first come to an agreement; I mean that the government should first come to terms with the provinces instead of holding a referendum and proposing an election under a sovereign government in a province.
The arbitrary use of this legislation could therefore contribute to perpetuate the endless federal-provincial disputes and God knows we have had a lot of them for many years. The federal government could brandish the weapon of the referendum if it could not reach an agreement with a province. That would further restrict the provincial governments' freedom of action, which is already quite weak, or weakened, I believe, through the present government's efforts to centralize. And that even if the bill stipulates that referenda would only be advisory by nature. The government would not be bound by the results.
So the government has recently been converted to referenda and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) states that it is fair and reasonable to consult the people. But if he really believes in the people's verdict, why is he not bound by the results? That may be because there were two referenda in Canada, one in 1898 on prohibition and the other in 1942 on conscription, and both have created immeasurable problems for the government and each time parliament had to pass legislation authorizing the government to hold a referendum.
I do not want to defend the old system, Mr. Speaker, but there is a limit to abuses which could have created the unregulated use of referenda. If it is so worth while to consult the people, why does the minister not allow referenda by petition? That is a procedure used regularly in Switzerland and several European countries. Then there was Howard Jarvis' famous Proposition 13 in California and I think everyone knows about that referendum.
So Bill C-9 is in many respects an all-purpose piece of legislation. That is why I want to express certain reservations I have with respect to this bill although 1 support its principle by and large.
I would like to deal for a few moments with the whole matter of the financial controls being established under this bill. As a result, any person could, without being registered, incur referendum expenses provided his or her contributions and expenses do not exceed $5,000. In the case of the Quebec legislation, individuals, whether severally or together, could only spend up to $300 for holding a meeting that is not organized by an umbrella organization. Contributions would be limited to $3,000 per voter and corporate persons would not be authorized to participate. Those contributions could still be paid directly to a political party.
In that respect, I feel the legislation we have before us encourages individual involvement.

On the other hand, under the Quebec legislation political parties could before the referendum raise up to $3,000 per voter and each umbrella organization could receive from the parties up to 25 cents per voter. Another limit of $3,000 per voter would apply to funds raised directly by umbrella organizations. Bill C-9 provides that funds earmarked for the referendum campaign could be raised by a party or a registered committee at any time after the tabling of the government's motion.
Mr. Speaker, a comparison between these two approaches reveals some inconsistency on the part of this government. First, they place a ceiling on individual and corporate spending but they do not on political parties.
Pursuant to another provision the government may refund part of the expenses incurred for election campaigns. The amount of the refund would be set once this provision is passed. But indeed, Mr. Speaker, would it not be better to set the rules of the game at this stage? Even the government is showing its political opportunism by trying to make a last minute decision on the reimbursements of referendum expenses. I do not know exactly what the Minister of Justice thinks about it, but I would simply ask him to set the rules of the game before the referendum takes place, not after.
Still the bill contains very clearcut provisions regarding radio and TV broadcasting.
Despite the critical remarks which I have made, I suggest that the referendum bill could turn out to be a necessary legislative instrument, both simple and efficient. Despite certain imperfections, most of the aspects of public consultation make sense. By not showing a preference for the establishment of umbrella organizations, this bill will make things easier for political parties which will not necessarily be forced to join a united front as is the case for the federalist parties in Quebec. Furthermore, referenda will be held within structures which are more or less similar to those provided for by electoral regulations and procedures.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to bring up the pros and cons of this bill. I perfectly agree on the need for a general law dealing with public consultations in Canada. However, just as many other members, I have an important reservation. In its present form, this bill might contribute to worsen the various confrontations and contentions on matters of jurisdiction which already exist between the federal and provincial governments. These confrontations could hurt the state of harmony in this country since they could lead to irreversible scissions. One must not forget the fact, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the man in the street who wants our country to be divided and is calling for a referendum. The farm hand, the unemployed, the worker, the housewife are not asking for a referendum, the only thing those people want to have is security in a great and beautiful country and bread and butter for tomorrow, as composer Tex Lecor would put it; "When Rosalie decides to put something in the fridge." speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) two straightforward questions concerning Canadian representation in the United States and the manner of parliamentary approval for any forthcoming Canadian commitment to a United Nations force in Namibia. Not surprisingly, 1 received the rhetorical splendour of the minister in response, but no factual answer. That leads to the deeper questions of the ad hoc management of Canada's foreign policy and the level of public information about that policy. Those are vital questions, as quickly became apparent at the foreign policy conference sponsored last weekend by the Progressive Conservative party.
At this important conference held at the Guild Inn, Toronto, 50 specialists in foreign policy, with academic, research, business, church and non-governmental organization backgrounds from across Canada, gathered to discuss the thematic issues of Canadian foreign policy for the 1980s: Canadian interests, security, human rights and development. Some 38 representatives of the diplomatic corps in Ottawa were present. Indeed this was a rare and valuable moment in the history of foreign policy in our country, and reveals the open manner of consultation by the Progressive Conservative party.
A major concern expressed at the conference was that our foreign policy has become confused, vague, and indecipherable by the public. This is not the fault of Department of External Affairs officers, whom I have found to be competent and dedicated. Rather, it is the fault of the government which is so overwhelmed by the national unity and domestic economy problems that it is unable to chart a clear course in foreign relations. To be responsive to the needs of our time, it is not necessary to conjure up grand designs or new slogans. It is necessary to build on the values, tradition and wisdom of our society, and explain to the Canadian people where we are going.
Adjournment Debate
Throughout the 1970s, we have been buffeted by one international shock wave after another: the OPEC price spiral, the escalating arms race, the north-south development imbalance, economic recession and protectionism, China's westward look, and the new demand for human rights. In the face of all these events the most distinguishing marks of Canadian foreign policy were the attempted diminishment of our deep relationship with the United States, the undercutting of our defence commitments with our NATO partners, and a slogan for something called "a contractual link". No wonder we give the impression we are wandering in a jungle at midnight without a compass. Is there some reason why the government fails to define and state clearly what our goals are in the changing global community?
Our conference last weekend was a success because we approached these questions systematically. For the past two years our party has been constructing a foreign policy built on the pillars of security, freer trade, human rights, and world development. With the added insights of the specialists who gave us their views, we believe we can give a sense of direction to Canadians for the 1980s, which sense of direction can be stated succinctly. We recognize we cannot separate our own domestic aspirations for peace, prosperity and social justice from the global questions of the arms race, nuclear proliferation, food and energy shortages, and human rights. Also we recognize worldwide co-operation institutions are not simply the sensible way to approach such problems, but are literally the only way. It is in Canada's interests to extend the security, freedoms and progress we enjoy through improving our global connection.
The priorities in this work are to strengthen our relationship with the United States, so that Canadian economic interests are represented more systematically at the highest levels of the American government. As a western nation, there should be no doubt that our defence requires an ungrudging commitment to NATO and NORAD. The Commonwealth and La Franco-phonie enable us to maintain the relationships which flow from our historical duality.
For Canadian foreign policy to be implemented in the 1980s, it will be necessary to have much more public support than is now apparent. This means opening up the process to the scrutiny of parliament, the media, and hence the public. I say with shame that in all of 1978 there was not one foreign policy debate in the House of Commons. The whole process today is so secret one would think foreign policy was the preserve of the elite.
Actually, Canadians from coast to coast can benefit from a constructive foreign policy that draws on the entrepreneurial instinct in Canada. This was precisely the point made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in his address at the conference. There is a great amount of business awaiting Canadians abroad, an important finding that the Leader of the Opposition made on his recent trip, and which I also found on a round the world trip last year. I believe the time has come to

January 30,1979
Adjournment Debate
involve the Canadian private sector in the implementation of foreign policy through stimulating more joint ventures in such areas as oil, rapeseed, fisheries, nuclear technology, STOL aircraft, and housing. There are vast opportunities ahead for more economic co-operation and trade generally. That is a direction for the 1980s that Canadians will support.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-SECOND READING OF BILL CONCERNING ARAB BOYCOTT
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-SECOND READING OF BILL CONCERNING ARAB BOYCOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked my question about the Arab boycott legislation proposed by the government because I think it is time to focus attention on it again, and I am convinced that this government may need to have a fire lit under it to get it to honour the commitment it has made to the Canadian people on this subject. What is the boycott? The Arab countries have banded together and agreed to try to prevent Israeli products from entering into their countries. As Canadians we may not like that, but it is the business of the Arab countries and Israel whether one wishes to trade with the other or not, and that is not an object of Canadian policy.
But there are two other dimensions to this boycott which are totally unacceptable to Canadians. The first dimension is that if a Canadian company wishes to trade with an Arab country, the boycott requires that it agree not to trade with Israel. This is an effort to create an international restraint of trade which would apply to the detriment of our economy, it is not in the national interest of, nor is it acceptable to Canada. The other dimension of the Arab boycott which is even more unacceptable is that it calls for discrimination within our own boundaries because the boycott requires that a company wanting to do business with Arab countries must give undertaking that Zionist firms, Jews or firms owned by Jews in our country will not be given any participation in those contracts and that the company will not hire Jews here.
Clearly, this is unacceptable in Canada, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was the first to say so when he was asked about it in this House in May, 1975. At that time he said that this aspect of the Arab boycott was against Canadian ethics and everything for which Canada stands. That is a statement with which all Canadians will agree.
The government then proceeded to implement a policy in an attempt to prevent the Arab boycott from having this terrible application to Canadian trade abroad and within Canada. It did not do what the United States did when the Arab boycott became an issue in that country. Legislation was presented which prevented American companies from complying with the boycott and required them to disclose when they were asked to do so. When the United States implemented that legislation they did not completely close the door to the boycott because the legislation does not apply to foreign subsidiaries of American corporations so, for example, an American subsidiary in Europe would be free to comply with the boycott.
[Mr. Roche.)
January 30, 1979

In Canada there is no comparable external dimension of economic activity under Canadian control. If we had enacted legislation of that sort it would have been much tougher in effect. The fact of the matter is, however, that Canada put forward a policy which sounded good on paper. We said that we would withhold government services and that we would require disclosure by companies of any efforts on the part of Arab countries to impose the boycott internally in Canada. But having said that, the policy seemed to disappear. There has been very little evidence to the Canadian people that that policy is in fact being implemented by the government. That was stage one.
Stage two was a commitment to introduce legislation to put some teeth behind the stage one policy, and that legislation is now on the order paper. I know that the Jewish community and others interested in civil liberties in Canadian society welcomed that legislation. I expected that it would be brought forward and implemented very quickly, but after many weeks since it was promised no action has been taken on it and second reading has not yet been proposed. I was very glad to hear the House leader say that he was prepared to consult with the parties on the other side to bring the legislation forward quickly. I hope he will do so, and I hope it will be soon.
I cannot sit down without adding that I am not satisfied with the legislation. It has some loopholes which require the attention of parliament. I hope it will be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for study. I do not like the discretion which it is proposed to give to the minister and which would permit him to grant exemptions and extensions to companies that may be in compliance with the boycott. Further, I think the penalty of $250 a day for failure to provide disclosure is a joke. It is not enough of a deterrent in a deal like the Bell Canada deal, although I do not know if the Arab boycott has been imposed there. The Human Rights Commission set up by parliament is now looking into that matter, a deal involving hundreds of millions of dollars. The idea that such a deal would be affected by a fine of $250 per day is a joke.
This legislation should be brought forward so that we can examine it and try to implement the spirit of the remarks made by the Prime Minister in 1975 to the effect that the Arab boycott is totally unacceptable. What is needed is strong legislation to deal with it so that Canadian values will be imposed on and reflected in Canadian trade abroad. I am sure that there is not an interest group in Canada that does not want us to trade with the Arabs. It is a big potential market, which we need. But we must pursue it with integrity.

I think we have to examine the bill. Specifically, the types of activities which the government finds unacceptable are those which would, in connection with the provisions of any international economic boycotts, require a Canadian firm or individual to engage in discrimination based on the race, national or ethnic origin or religion of any Canadian firm or individual; refuse to purchase from or sell to any other Canadian firm or individual; refuse to sell Canadian goods to any country; refrain from purchases from any country; or restrict commercial investment or other economic activity in any country.
More specifically, this legislation would require any Canadian person who receives a prescribed boycott request to report such a request to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) within 30 days of receipt of the request. Furthermore, those persons who comply with the request are obliged to report such fact to the minister within ten days. Failure to report will be punishable by a fine of $250 for each day late in reporting the required information. This amounts to some $90,000 for anyone who fails to report for one year, which is a stiff penalty indeed.
As per current practice, the minister will table semi-annually a report providing a statistical summary of the information filed, as well as the names of those persons who have complied with prescribed boycott requests. Regulations by order in council which have been tabled in the House on December 15 will prescribe those foreign boycotts requests that need be reported. It is not the government's intention to require reporting of primary boycott requests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we seem to be getting long answers from the government side tonight. I hope that I will not break the mould.
I am rising because of a question that I asked last week of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). Another minister was asked a supplementary question. First of all, I asked a question concerning the fall of the Cosmos and

January 30, 1979
Adjournment Debate
the subsequent bill. In Hansard for January 24, 1979, at page 2512,1 asked the minister to explain:
-why the government failed to claim under Treaty 6 where under article 5, paragraph 5, the Soviets would have been required to pay all expenses incurred in the recovery of returning space objects?
To this, the Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
Mr. Speaker, I will as soon as I get a chance to look at Treaty 6.
He went on to say:
I have to tell the hon. member that I have relied upon the advice of our legal experts on this matter. It was their judgment that this was the proper and appropriate way to proceed. I must confess that, not being a legal person myself, I do not know what the answer is to the hon. member's question.
He was not the only minister whose ignorance was all too apparent. I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) what the total cost of the operation was. His department was responsible for the last and longest part of the search and clean up operation. The minister took no less than nine lines of Hansard to inform the House that he did not know what his department's claim was, or that of any other department whose operations he had been responsible for co-ordinating.
The sad part of this ministerial ignorance is the history behind it. The performance of the ministers in particular has revealed a far from adequate level of knowledge and ability to act in the best interests of Canada. What is worse is that there is no evidence that they have yet learned anything from their previous mistakes.
In January, 1978, a similar series of questions was asked. At that time neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) nor the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) could do anything about the possible crash of the satellite until a few moments before it fell, despite the fact the Prime Minister had been at Norad headquarters and received what he said was a complete briefing on the matter. In the early days of the crisis it was revealed that there was no grasp of the dimensions of the problem, or how to exercise existing treaties to which Canada and the U.S.S.R. are both parties. To this day there is a lack of understanding of the two simple treaties that govern this matter.
Treaty 6 covers expenses of recovering satellites or parts of satellites. Treaty 7 covers damage that might be incurred by a satellite. We are in the peculiar position of having used up a lot of money for the recovery of parts of the satellite. Obviously this should come under Treaty 6 which covers expenses. In fact in one place it has the words "expenses of the search". Treaty 7 which covers damages is meant to cover damage to buildings or to a city if a satellite crash lands, or indeed damage to another aircraft; it makes provision for that.
When I asked the ministers if they had read the treaties they made light of it, or claimed they were too difficult to read. People who write bills for this government should study the English in these treaties. They are the easiest and shortest I have seen for a long time. Treaty 6, which no one on the government side seems to have read yet, contains only three pages, and is written in crystal clear English. It is not the fact that they did not have sufficient warning on this matter. Last

January, 1978, when the satellite fell, my first question to the ministers was with respect to the Cosmos satellite. As reported at page 2347 of Hansard I asked:
-has the Canadian government notified the U.S.S.R. of the discovery on our soil of a space object, or its component parts, believed to be of a hazardous or deleterious nature, as we are required to do under article 5 of the international agreement on the return of objects launched into outer space?
This is in the treaty we should have been claiming under. However, we have to notify them. This we were not doing. The Minister of National Defence replied:
The international regime will meet its responsibilities, as was indicated to the Department of External Affairs by the Soviet ambassador.
In other words, do not worry about the bills, the U.S.S.R. will pay them. When I asked if indeed they had filed under another provision of the treaty, the minister replied, "not to the best of my knowledge." On February 1 I again asked if they had filed under the appropriate section. The Minister of National Defence replied:
There has been no request for Russian assistance from any of our people. The Soviets have offered to assist, but there has not been a need for it.
On February 3 I asked:
Did the government formally notify the Soviet Union, as we are required to do under clause 4 of article 5 of the treaty governing the return of objects launched into space, and have the Soviets responded in the manner they were obliged to do if we so informed them that an object of a hazardous and deleterious nature had crashed in our territory?
The Minister of National Defence replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions between officials of the Department of External Affairs and the Soviet government to determine the consequences of this.
I then asked:

The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the treaty has been exercised in that manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue raised this evening by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) is important and therefore would require much more time than I am allowed. I would however take this opportunity to repeat the assurances given by my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) in this House on December 14. Hon. members will recall the minister indicated at that time that our NATO allies welcomed our efforts.
January 30, 1979

Hon. members will also recall the minister recently visited Canadian troups in Germany. Dr. Apel, the minister in charge of national defence in the Federal Republic of Germany joined Mr. Danson for that visit. Both ministers visited Canadian military facilities in Lahr and Baden, and after private and public talks Dr. Apel paid tribute to the Canadian contribution. Later in the course of that trip, the minister visited Greece, another NATO ally, where important and very positive meetings were held. During those meetings with representatives of other NATO countries, it was sensed that the Canadian contribution is very well recognized. Canadian soldiers of both sexes are truly professionals, and I believe that all hon. members here share this view. This is a recognized fact in the NATO organization, the United Nations and everywhere else. We are now in the process of buying the best kind of equipment that will allow our forces to show their ability and complete their training. Mr. Speaker, two especially interesting events occurred last week, one in London, Ontario, and the other in Burbank, California. In London, it was the AVGP, a
Adjournment Debate
multiple purpose vehicle. This vehicle was preceded by the Leopard tanks which are now in Gagetown, New Brunswick. The AVGP will be used to train our armoured force, and because of its multiple role, it will also be used by our troops. In Burbank, it was the Aurora. This airplane has the reputation of being the best in the world. Eighteen of these airplanes will be purchased from the Lockheed Company in California. The first will be delivered in May 1980 and the last one in March 1981.
I could give many other examples, Mr. Speaker, such as the progress accomplished in our fighter plane purchasing program and the new shipbuilding project for our fleet. What is important to note, Mr. Speaker, is the quality of our equipment and the professionalism of our people, which are both recognized by NATO.
